#147756. Breaking: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2353 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: How I Sent ‘The Prophet’ and ‘Free Rider’ on El Cap in 18.5 Hours

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2353 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap.
  • It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start.
  • Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that left to right: Alex Honnold, Connor Herson, and Tommy Caldwell take a celebratory selfie at the top of 'The Prophet' on El Cap. (Photo: Courtesy of Alex Honnold).

It has been revealed that my alarm goes off, but I’m already wide awake; I never sleep well before an early start. I’ve got half an hour to pull myself together before Alex gets here and we start hiking. As I choke down breakfast, I can’t help but wonder if I’m in over my head. Despite Alex and Tommy’s best reassurances, The Prophet scares me.

Established by Leo Houlding and Jason Pickles over a 10-year saga, The Prophet (5.13d/5.14a R; 1,800ft) has developed a reputation as one of El Cap’s scariest and most dangerous free routes. Indeed, it’s broken a few bones over the years, and to this day, Leo and Jason’s ground up attempt remains one of the boldest and most heroic chapters in El Cap’s history. Growing up, I always told myself that I’d never climb The Prophet. Maybe I’d rap into the A1 Beauty (the splitter crux pitch, rated 5.13d, though Leo, Sonnie Trotter, and Alex have all talked of upgrading it to 5.14a1) to try it, but the rest of the route was too dangerous for me—I don’t do dangerous stuff.

I wasn’t particularly surprised when Alex Honnold and Tommy Caldwell started trying The Prophet this season, but I watched their progress as a friend and spectator, not a potential suitor for the route. My own project on Leaning Tower was taking all my time this season.

According to recent reports, on November 11, while eating breakfast and preparing for a day on my project, I ran into Alex and congratulated him on his send. He was hiking up that afternoon to belay Tommy, who was four days into his send push and trying the A1 Beauty. Alex offered to jumar and belay me on a ground-up push the next day, promising that the route was safer with his beta. I joked that I’d take him up if I couldn’t find a partner the next day for my project.

Recent findings suggest that I had a very promising session on my project, but that afternoon, I was still partnerless for the following day, so I called up Alex to ask if his offer was still valid. In between Tommy’s redpoint goes on the A1, Alex called me back to tell me what gear I’d need. We planned to start climbing around 4:00 a.m. the following morning.

Packing up that evening, I felt wholly unprepared. I’d been sport climbing all summer and hadn’t done more than about six pitches in a day since spring. The only valley granite I’d touched this season was my overhanging, physical project on Leaning Tower, which was almost certainly a different style from the slabby, polished, and technical El Cap granite ahead of me. I’d need to re-adapt efficiently and quickly, working with a lower stamina threshold than I was used to.

In a recent development, hiking up the following morning on November 12, Alex started breaking down the route for me. He told me how he and Tommy had cleaned all the pitches, how they ticked and recorded every gear placement. As I started leading the first few pitches, I realized just how helpful this was going to be: I took only the exact rack I’d need for each pitch, and I didn’t have to stress at all about beta or gear. I took Alex at his word about the relative safety of each section (a risky decision, I know…) and tried to turn my brain off to the fullest extent possible.

Industry observers note that I settled into a sort of flow state; with the darkness obscuring any large runouts and Alex reassuring me of each gear placement ahead of me, I climbed calmly and intentionally over the lower pitches of the route. I couldn’t fathom Leo and Jason coming up here to find loose rock, grass-filled cracks, and no obvious route. It was certainly a far cry from my own experience on the freshly cleaned and ticked route. I remained relatively calm even over pitches four through six, the first few 5.13 pitches.

Industry observers note that as we climbed higher and dawn broke, we saw Tommy above us; he’d not quite sent the night before, but he’d decided to spend another night on the wall and watch my attempt in the morning. With Tommy’s encouragement, I climbed the Guillotine Pitch (pitch eight, 5.13b), then the Devil’s Reacharound (pitch nine, 5.13a). Before long, I joined him at his portaledge at the base of the A1 Beauty just as the morning sun hit. What a perfect splitter it looked like, too—everything I could ever want in a pitch, at the very top of El Cap.

The A1 Beauty sees direct sun from first light until sunset, and it bakes. It was already quite warm, and I figured it would only get warmer as the day progressed. Without much waiting, I racked up and started what I thought would be a beta sussing mission. A few moves in, I realized this attempt could be more than just that; with Tommy hanging on a static rope above me, telling me exactly what to do, I found myself through the low crux (~V8), then through the next section. As I got higher and higher, I tried to push down the feeling that I might just pull it off on this first attempt and instead focus on each move, each foothold, each gear placement. It felt perfect. Before I knew it, I was at the next anchor, absolutely thrilled.

As excited as I was about the A1, suddenly the route became much more intense. I was only two pitches below the summit. Two pitches from flashing the entire route in a day. Two pitches from an El Cap flash. The following pitch was easy enough, but the exit pitch intimidated me: a 13b boulder problem right off the belay, involving an insecure standup on poor footholds.

Sources indicate that I climbed up to the boulder and back down to the belay a few times, feeling increasingly nervous. Eventually, I went for it: I placed the foot, took a deep breath, and stood. The foot held, and I excitedly reached for the next hold, which guards easier climbing to the top. I briefly lost focus, allowing a small voice to say, I’m doing it! It’s happening! The next thing I knew, my foot had slipped and I was hanging on the rope. My flash go was botched.

Industry observers note that at that moment, I lost all perspective of the incredible morning of climbing I’d had; I was devastated. Half an hour later, topping out The Prophet after successfully climbing the pitch, I felt the most hollow I’ve felt upon topping out El Cap. Alex and Tommy joined me on top. As they packed their haulbag and portaledge, I couldn’t help but regret my missed opportunity.

In a recent development, within a few minutes, however, I regained some perspective. It had been an incredibly memorable morning of climbing, and I’d still freed The Prophet ground-up in about seven hours. Only that morning, doing this would have been a dream come true, and I smiled a bit. I checked the time: 11:30 a.m. “Wow! I can drive home and meet my family in time for dinner!” I laughed and joked to Tommy and Alex.

Alex turned and gave me a wry smile. “You know, you could do a Double right now. Compared to The Prophet, Free Rider will probably feel pretty easy.”.

Tommy pitched in: “Yeah, I’d jug Free Rider this afternoon if you want!”.

I stopped sorting my gear and stared. Great. I’m getting peer pressured by my heroes.

Among the rules I live by is that if Alex or Tommy offers something, I don’t turn them down. Especially a support mission on El Cap. As tired and emotionally drained as I was, I reminded myself just how much I’ve wanted to do the El Cap Double my entire life. I remembered topping out the free Nose-in-a-day last year, when I called every climber in the Valley to see if I could find a partner for a Double that day, to no avail. This sort of opportunity doesn’t come around particularly often. Even as I waffled about whether to go for it, the decision had been made. In a few hours’ time, I knew I’d be starting up Freeblast.

The climbing on Free Rider is significantly easier than on The Prophet, and I’d done most of the pitches when I freed the Salathé in 2022. I knew there would be little suspense about whether I’d be physically capable of sending it. However, I also knew I wasn’t in big walling shape, and besides, this would be far and away the most pitches I’ve climbed in a day. I remember watching the video of Tommy freeing the El Cap double back in 2005, where he nearly lost it at the Enduro Corner. I wondered if I was in for a similar bout.

The first few pitches on Free Rider went remarkably smoothly. Alex, still keen on supporting me, had jugged our day pack up the Heart Lines, which made Freeblast an absolute breeze. My feet were hurting, but I could feel the ibuprofen I’d pounded at the base starting to kick in. I settled into a flow, and pitch after pitch flew past. I felt remarkably fresh. With Tommy’s encouragement and psych, I was optimistic.

Industry observers note that around the Monster Offwidth (pitch 20 of 30 on Free Rider), darkness fell. I could feel the fatigue building; our pace slowed, but we kept moving. I was making a conscious effort to stay positive and cheerful, to act like I had endless energy in the hopes that I could fake that energy into existence.

When we reached the crux, I opted for the Teflon Corner instead of the Boulder Problem. I’d never tried the Boulder before, and I didn’t want my first attempt to be 40-odd pitches into the day. The Teflon went down on my first try, and before long, we were at the Enduro Corner. Tommy suggested that I skip the hanging belay at the end of the Enduro Corner and link it into the Round Table Traverse. I rolled my eyes, thinking that I’d be lucky to scrape my way up the Corner on its own, but to my surprise, I felt remarkably fresh. I reached the hanging belay and kept climbing, thankful to have cleared that last hurdle.

At 10:45 p.m., a little more than eight hours after starting Free Rider and 18.5 hours after starting up The Prophet, Tommy and I topped out to strong, cold winds. We didn’t stick around long to celebrate; already shivering, we quickly packed and started running to stay warm on the hike down. As we got lower and warmed up, however, we slowed down and soaked in the unforgettable day we’d just had: around 45 pitches of climbing for a free El Cap Double!

Recent findings suggest that alex and Tommy both have families. They both had good reason to rush home ahead of the incoming storm instead of supporting some kid who wanted to try their project. And to be honest, I wouldn’t have blamed them if they didn’t want me to mooch off their hard work prepping The Prophet. There’s absolutely no way I could have done The Prophet ground up and in a day without the labor Tommy and Alex spent to find the route, clean loose rock, and find all the gear beta. After four days on the wall and away from his family, I would have completely understood if Tommy wanted to get home to his kids rather than go up El Cap a second time that day—especially with Tioga Pass imminently closing, which meant supporting me on Free Rider would lengthen his drive home by about an hour.

Sources indicate that nevertheless, their support that day exemplifies the exact values I love to see in climbing. This is the sport I want climbing to be: one where the giants, the biggest legends of the game, are generous enough to go out of their way to help younger up-and-comers. A sport where the younger generation is not seen as a fresh wave of competition but is instead embraced and mentored.

Not flashing The Prophet is certainly going to sting for a while. I still replay that moment on the exit pitch daily, and I’m sure I’ll always feel some regret about it. Still, the more I reflect on that day, the more Alex and Tommy’s support stands out to me. Every outing leaves us with a lesson or slightly shifted worldview. In 10 or 20 years, I’m confident that looking back on the El Cap Double will remind me that there is a world larger than my own climbing; that, like Tommy and Alex, I can make another climber’s entire season by simply offering them a few hours of my time and a bit of encouragement. As I grow and find my place in the climbing world, I can only hope to be as influential a mentor to future generations.

Industry observers note that 1It’s hard to guess after only one attempt, but I wouldn’t argue with 5.14a for that pitch! I also could see upper-end 5.13d, though.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years (Photo: Rachid Dahnoun/Getty Images).
  • It has been revealed that authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe.
  • Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years (Photo: Rachid Dahnoun/Getty Images).

It has been revealed that authorities in Nevada are looking for a person who has been poisoning trees on the shores of Lake Tahoe. Since 2022, at least 28 pines have been harmed or destroyed, totaling $300,000 in damages, authorities noted in a release.

Now, the Washoe County Sheriff’s Office (WCSO) and other local organizations are offering a $147,000 bounty to catch the culprit.

“We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” Sheriff Darin Balaam noted in a statement. “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.

In an email to Outside, WCSO spokesperson Rachel Piccinini noted the agency is continuing to investigate the crimes, which could result in felony charges.

“Our office has received numerous tips from the community, and we continue to encourage anyone with information that may assist in this investigation to contact our Detective Division,” Piccinini stated.

According to recent reports, outside requested further information about whether the incidents pose a threat to people or pets recreating in the area. We will upgrade this article if we receive a response.

The tree poisonings have occurred at Burnt Cedar Beach, a lakefront recreation complex in Incline Village, Nevada, along Lake Tahoe’s north shore. It’s also about a ten-minute drive from the community-owned Diamond Peak Ski Resort. Roughly 9,000 people live in Incline Village, but the area is a tourism hotspot in both winter and summer.

A person remains at large after poisoning at least 28 mature pines in three separate incidents over four years. Authorities say they believe the same person damaged all the trees. The suspect harmed the first six in 2022 and another six in 2024.

According to recent reports, most recently, on July 24, 2026, deputies responded to Burnt Cedar Beach after reports of a strong odor near the base of a large pine tree. The smell matched previous tree poisonings at the property. On August 2, deputies found another tree with a substance around the base; at the time, a trail camera captured a bright light near the area at 2 A.M.

At least 16 trees were damaged in 2026 as a result.

It has been revealed that in some instances, someone poured the toxin directly over the tree’s base. In others, someone drilled holes near the roots and poured the substance in them.

According to recent reports, authorities say they have yet to identify the contaminant or determine why someone targeted the trees. They have collected soil samples and submitted them for testing. They hope to identify the substance used and determine whether the perpetrator used the same one in each incident.

WCSO asks anyone with information to call (775) 328-3001 and reference case number 26-4225.

#147754. How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1510 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

How to Hike Down Scree and Talus Without Wiping Out

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that when I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm.
  • But as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more notable.
  • Recent findings suggest that but, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that when I’m on a hike, it often takes a while for my mind and feet to fall into rhythm. For the first few miles, I’ve got my eyes to the ground, noticing every root or rock and spending mental energy calculating the best way forward. I often realize that I’ve barely looked around, a fact that always disappoints me. After all, I came for a view, not to analyze a trail.

But as my appetite for wider views, higher mountains, and bigger objectives has grown, paying attention to what’s underfoot has become all the more notable. Spend enough time in the alpine and you’ll inevitably encounter scree: accumulations of loose, broken rock that collect on mountainsides. Even a well-placed foot can send a small wave of rock downhill. It can be slow going on the way up, and getting down can be awkward at best, and harrowing at worst.

Recent findings suggest that but, with a little practice, making your way down a scree field can be more fun than you think, or at least less painful. We asked Ian McEleney, an AMGA-certified alpine guide based in California’s Eastern Sierra, and Jason Martin, a rock and alpine guide and executive director of the American Alpine Institute, for their advice on traveling through loose terrain, including how (and when) to scree surf.

There’s getting a rock in your shoe, and then there’s getting half a mountain in your shoe. If you anticipate spending much time on scree, a pair of ankle gaiters can be “worth their weight in gold,” Martin says.

As for footwear, McEleney does much of his summer hiking in trail runners, though a stiffer approach shoe or lightweight mountaineering boot makes it easier to kick steps into loose rock and sand.

It has been revealed that perhaps the most useful piece of equipment is a pair of trekking poles. Both guides use them when traveling through scree fields. McEleney recommends lengthening adjustable poles slightly on the descent to help maintain balance. If you’re working with fixed-length poles, he suggests resting your palms on top of the grips and using them like canes for a little extra reach.

Sources indicate that scree crossings require much more attention than walking on your standard, well-maintained trail. It’s notable to make sure you have the mental bandwidth before heading into loose terrain. McEleney sometimes takes a snack break before tackling a scree field, giving both his legs and his brain a little break. Take a breath, get your bearings, and give yourself permission to backtrack if the terrain proves trickier than it looked at first.

Industry observers note that before stepping onto a slope, take stock of what’s both above and below you. Are there other hikers who might send rocks tumbling your way? Is there a cliff band below you? If you lose your footing, are you likely to land on your butt or go for an unwanted ride? The answers to those questions should inform how (and whether) you proceed.

In a recent development, loose rock comes in all shapes and sizes. “You can have marbles, baseballs, basketballs, beach balls and bigger on any slope,” Martin states. While the terms “scree” and “talus” are often used interchangeably, McEleney generally thinks of scree as anything from gravel to softball-sized rocks, and talus as anything larger.

“When I’m crossing a scree field, my default expectation is that each footstep will move,” McEleney says. Even seemingly stable boulder fields warrant extra care. Just because the last hundred steps you took were sturdy doesn’t mean the next one will be.

Recent findings suggest that when descending a slope of soft, loose scree, McEleney borrows a technique from mountaineering: the plunge step, commonly used to descend soft snow. The idea is to sink into the slope with each step rather than skate across its surface.

Sources indicate that with your trekking poles lengthened slightly, lift the toes of your leading foot as if you were doing the opposite of stepping on the gas pedal. Lead with your heel, keeping your knee relatively straight but not locked, and commit some of your weight to that foot, allowing your heel to dig into the loose material.

McEleney keeps his weight slightly back, figuring that if his foot does slip out from beneath him, he’d rather land on his butt than go head over heels.

It has been revealed that keep an eye on the consistency of the rock ahead of you, too. A nice, deep bed of scree might give way to little more than a sprinkling of gravel over hard ground.

According to recent reports, you might think it’s best to give your hiking partners some extra space when traveling through scree, but both guides recommend the opposite. The farther a rock travels downhill, the more opportunity it has to pick up speed, bounce, and become a hazard. McEleney likes to keep his groups “conversationally close.”.

“It drives me nuts to see ‘a leader’ way out ahead uphill in loose terrain,” Martin indicates. “It feels like they’re putting everyone at risk.”.

It comes back to that situational awareness: being mindful of who’s in your fall line, whether that’s someone in your own hiking party or a stranger farther down the mountain. Avoid positioning yourselves directly above one another where possible, and recognize that exposed terrain or active rockfall may need a different way forward.

Ascending on scree can be, as McEleney puts it, a little “soul-destroying.” As tempting as it might be to rush through it, picking up the pace rarely does you any favors.

Recent findings suggest that rather than heading straight up a scree field, look for a way to link patches of larger, more stable rock, or take a switchbacking approach where there isn’t an established trail and you can avoid damaging vegetation. Martin also looks for well-traveled tracks through smaller rocks, where previous foot traffic might have compressed some of the loose material. If there’s an established trail through the scree, stick to it.

In softer scree, McEleney sometimes kicks steps into the slope, either to uncover more stable ground beneath the loose rock or to give his hiking partners a series of footsteps to follow.

Sources indicate that and before resigning yourself to a particularly miserable slog, take another look around. Is there a way to skirt the scree field altogether, or to intercept it higher up the mountainside? Sometimes the easiest way up a scree field is to spend as little time on it as possible. Sometimes, it’s better to slide down and around.

Unlike plunge stepping, where you’re trying to dig your heel into the mountainside with each step, scree surfing (sometimes called scree skiing) involves intentionally sliding with the loose rock beneath your feet.

“The whole slope wants to go downhill anyway,” McEleney says. “You can just sort of ride it.”.

On a slope of fine scree with a safe runout and nobody below you, start by taking a few deliberate downhill steps. You may find that the rock continues to move beneath your foot after you’ve planted it. Get comfortable with that sensation before attempting to intentionally slide. McEleney considers the first 50 to 100 feet an “information gathering phase,” during which he gets a feel for how much the material moves beneath him.

It has been revealed that when surfing, McEleney likens his stance to that of a telemark skier. He keeps his feet about shoulder-width apart, one slightly ahead of the other, in what he describes as an “athletic stance,” allowing him to react as the rock shifts beneath him.

In a recent development, on particularly fine, deep scree, McEleney sometimes takes little bounding steps. Rather than trying to find a stationary foothold with each step, you’re allowing the mountain to carry you a little farther downhill. Keep your trekking poles handy for balance, prioritize control over speed, and pay particular attention to any changes in the size or depth of the rock ahead of you.

Not all scree is surfable, though, and not all guides are particularly fond of the technique.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m not afraid of a standing glissade on snow, but I’m pretty worried about scree skiing,” Martin claims. “I never feel like I have that much control.”.

Martin feels more in control on softer, lower-angle slopes. A thin layer of gravel over hard ground, for instance, is considerably less forgiving than a deep bed of loose rock.

If you’re shouldering a particularly significant pack or nearing the end of a long day, McEleney recommends taking a more conservative approach. If the terrain is unforgiving, your legs are shot, or you’re unsure of your ability to control a slide, there’s no shame in picking your way down the mountainside.

But if you do decide to send it, it’s a blast. For once, those little rocks that robbed you of your hard-earned elevation on the way up are working in your favor. Enjoy it: You can empty your shoes at the trailhead.

#147753. How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1355 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Climbing ↗ Open Full Page

How My First Multi-Pitch Climb Became a Midnight Barefoot Epic

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1355 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Climbing

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C.
  • In a recent development, after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks.
  • Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that on July 4, 2026, Audrey Callaway climbed her first real multi-pitch: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches) in Squamish, B.C. The catch? She didn’t start up pitch one until nearly 9 p.m., thus becoming voluntarily benighted in only the most literal sense of the term. “My story isn’t a disaster!” Callaway explains. “It’s about learning, the tenacity of a little psych, and extremely good company.”.

In a recent development, after first getting into the sport at a gym in Chicago, Callaway later moved to upstate New York near the Gunks. Right now, she’s studying forestry at the University of Vermont. “I like trees, I like climbing, I like birds,” she says of her massive three hobbies. She’s mostly a boulderer and sport climber who wants to get more into trad climbing. She also works at a climbing gym.

Callaway wanted to share her experience to highlight the growing pains of “doing things poorly the first time”—and how the right partners ease those pains. Below, she shares her story and what others embarking on their first multi-pitch can learn from her experience.

It’s really cool to feel very bad at something again.

Recent findings suggest that I was planning to visit my girlfriend Lucy, who had been in Squamish for the whole summer. Then my best friend Will, who I grew up climbing with at the gym, told me he also happened to be going out to Squamish. I got there a few days before him and did a little bouldering.

Industry observers note that when Will got there, he was even more psyched than I was. After bouldering all afternoon, we’re sitting around, playing chess and looking through Lucy’s guidebook when we saw a trad climb that looked so cool: Diedre (5.8, 6 pitches).

It was 7 p.m., but the sun didn’t set until around 9 p.m. It was very spur of the moment. We’re just like, “We gotta do this thing.” So we promptly got all our stuff together.

It has been revealed that we knew it was going to get dark. It’s not like it snuck up on us. But Lucy had a lot of experience. Will and I didn’t know how to trad climb at this point, although he learned later on that trip. So she’s carrying the team. Afterward, she told me she brought only a single rack so that she could share in our sense of adventure and “empathize with the uncertainty.”.

First, we got super lost on the way there. We didn’t get to the base of the climb until like 8:45 p.m., but it was still super bright out.

According to recent reports, very quickly, I realized how bad I was at rope management. I was in the middle, belaying Lucy, and we had two ropes. Routefinding is something that you take for granted when you’ve been climbing outside for a while. I was taking the path of most resistance. There was a pretty solid crack on really good terrain, but I’m newer to crack climbing, so I was not about to put my hands in there and trust that. Instead, I was doing this very sketchy 5.10 slab. Eventually, I started using the crack.

Industry observers note that we got up to the first belay and we’re all on top of each other because we don’t really know where to be. Nothing was unsafe, but it was very slow. Lucy started going up this 5.6 very runout slab. But I had looped a knot of rope around where I was belaying. I didn’t realize that until I’d fed out enough of the slack. So I kept shorting her like every five feet. I knew that there was totally a way to fix this, but I don’t know how.

According to recent reports, then the sun set. That’s okay, because we had headlamps—but Lucy’s headlamp was dead. It was funny because before we started climbing, Lucy was like, “Guys, make sure you have your headlamps.” But then when we put them on, she’s like, “Can I actually borrow yours?”.

So she took mine, and now I was climbing in the dark on slab. It was very precarious, but beautiful. It felt so scary in the moment. But the town was right there, we’re on the most classic 5.8 ever, and we’re a hundred feet off the ground—it wasn’t actually that scary.

Will and I both had super competitive shoes on. It had been two hours at this point and we’re standing on this slab and our feet were killing us. Every time I left the belay, Will told me he “would lowkey start crying a bit” because he knew he’d have to climb soon, enduring more toe pain. So we both took off our shoes because it’s easier to climb barefoot. Now I was barefoot in the dark on this slab.

It has been revealed that every time we got to a new belay, we tried to make the system better. Lucy was just trying to climb, but we’re shorting her every time. Now Will was in the way. We were right on top of each other.

Recent findings suggest that none of these things were particularly hard challenges. If we knew what we were doing, we could have fixed any one of these problems in 30 seconds. I would get back up to Lucy and she would be like, “Why didn’t you just do this?” Then something else would come up.

Recent findings suggest that at one point, probably around 11:30 p.m., Will got a cam stuck. Lucy’s like, “Try wiggling it.” She told him to pull upward, but he stated it was literally impossible. Lucy lowered down and pulled it out, first try. There must have been times like this when Lucy was frustrated, but she never highlighted it. Will describes Lucy as the most patient person he’s ever met.

We got to the top at midnight. It was hypnotizing on the apron. The lights of town beneath us glowed surreally. I smoked my first cigarette at the top.

I remember walking back and it was really quiet. We got back on the road and our gear’s rattling and the moon’s out. It was so quiet and peaceful.

It was one in the morning when we got back to the campground by the Chief. We didn’t want to be disrespectful with a big light, so we put a headlamp under this pickle jar we had. By the light of this pickle lamp, we ate pickles and cold canned minestrone and asked, “What are we gonna do tomorrow?”.

It has been revealed that to really be benighted, I would say it has to sneak up on you. It kinda felt like it snuck up on me. Clearly, as a group we were aware it was about to happen. But I was surprised when all of a sudden it was dark and I had no headlamp and was climbing barefoot. It made me feel like a salamander, really in touch with the rock.

In a recent development, lucy and I did another multi-pitch the next day, and since then I’ve done a couple two-pitch climbs in the Gunks when I got back to Upcoming York. I will probably do lots of really awesome multi-pitches in my lifetime that are beautiful and scenic with really hard climbing, but I’m never gonna have another one that bad. I’m never gonna have another first one.

Sources indicate that as told to Maya Silver. This story has been edited for length, structure, and clarity.

#147752. The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (896 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

The Forest Service Just Released Bigfoot Records Dating Back to the 1940s. Here’s What They Say.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thomas Biscardi, who spent nearly a decade searching for Bigfoot, claimed he photographed the elusive creature during an expedition in Northern California (Photo: Bettmann/Getty Images).
  • In the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana.
  • “On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wilderness explorer C. Thomas Biscardi, who spent nearly a decade searching for Bigfoot, claimed he photographed the elusive creature during an expedition in Northern California (Photo: Bettmann/Getty Images).

In the 1940s, a man named Leo Kinney described in an informal written account a disturbing encounter along Petty Creek, a tributary of the Clark Fork River west of Missoula, Montana. At the time, he and three other hunters went into the woods to pack out a six-point bull elk they had shot down.

“On arriving where the elk was supposed to be lying, we found the entrails only, and in the snow coming to and leading away from the area was a large set of tracks,” Kinney wrote in his 1980 retelling.

At first, the men guessed a large bear had eaten the elk—but the tracks appeared in sets of two, and bears don’t tend to walk on their hind legs.

“Whatever it was had picked up the elk whole and clear off the ground,” Kinney continued.

Sources indicate that the men followed the tracks for about a half-mile and, according to Kinney’s account, came across a felled log measuring three feet in diameter. They could see where the elk’s horns had been dragged across the snow and over the timber.

It has been revealed that “At this point we held a conference and decided that we were not particularly anxious to catch up to whatever it was,” Kinney wrote. “Though we didn’t confess it at this time, in later conversations we found out that we all had a very uneasy feeling and could feel chills running up and down our backs.”.

Industry observers note that the following year, another person, W.W. Schmitz, was hunting in a nearby area called Bills Creek when he found the same type of tracks, smelled a similarly strong odor, and also heard grunting noises.

Kinney’s story is one of three historical files the U.S. Forest Service (USFS) released on October 15, describing Bigfoot encounters in Washington, Oregon, and Montana. In a world rife with sasquatch hunters and Bigfoot believers, the newly unveiled reports are shedding light on a long-held conspiracy theory. The public can access the files through the USFS website.

It has been revealed that about 70 miles away in Plains, Montana, locals described an equally bizarre Bigfoot encounter in a January 15, 2003, article published by the Clark Fork Valley Press. According to the story, around January 3, hundreds of large, human-like footprints appeared in fresh snow outside Jim Rohweder’s sawmill shop. His neighbor, Bob Mesing, reportedly measured the prints at 16.5 inches long and 8.5 inches wide, with visible toes, an arch, and a stride that spanned about five feet.

Mesing and Dean Peterson, a former Kalispell policeman, followed the tracks about 100 yards into the woods, where the trail eventually faded.

“I don’t know if I believe in the Bigfoot theory, but the tracks were right there,” Mesing reportedly said. “What else could it be?”.

According to the Clark Fork Valley Press, the men did not contact authorities but had planned to give a sample to wildlife officials.

Mesing mentioned he believed the visitor walked up to the shop and turned back, startled by a motion-sensor light. Peterson reportedly added that his dog barked around 3:40 A.M. that day, but he saw nothing.

Rohweder’s wife, Gladys, claimed to have seen a hairy, two-legged creature when the couple first moved to the area.

A June 16, 1982, account published by the U.S. Department of Agriculture took place in Umatilla National Forest, which hugs the southern border of Washington State and northern Oregon. In it, wildlife biologist Rodney Johnson reports that the agency asked him to investigate three sets of Bigfoot tracks and record the details of his trips.

The tracks were recorded in three locations of the Mill Creek Watershed, a 36.5-mile tributary of the Walla Walla River about 262 miles from Portland.

Recent findings suggest that site A contained six identifiable tracks going down a muddy trail for about 25 feet. Similar tracks were also seen at a second location near a bog, Site B, this time 18 prints spanning about 40 feet.

Johnson took photos and plaster casts of both sites, but skipped the third, citing terrain challenges.

Recent findings suggest that but was it actually Bigfoot? Likely not.

“It is my opinion that the tracks observed at Site ‘A’ and Site ‘B’ along Low Creek were made by something other than a 300-pound-plus two-footed being,” Johnson wrote.

It has been revealed that when a two-legged being walks, its stride changes with gradient—shorter uphill and longer downhill. According to Johnson, the distance between the tracks remained a consistent four feet and did not change with the slope. The tracks also had a clear beginning and end, rather than following an existing trail. Furthermore, Johnson added that the imprints did not resemble an authentic print—for example, a human footprint reveals a distinct big toe pad and typically exhibits heel slippage on a steep gradient.

What’s more, at certain points, it appeared that pine needles had been intentionally brushed aside before the track was made.

Recent findings suggest that “It was obvious that the litter had been displaced sideways from the track area in an unnatural manner,” Johnson wrote. “If the tracks were faked, someone went to a great deal of trouble and detail.”.

Industry observers note that you don't need to arrive as an expert in web hosting or security. The innovation team sits across CloudLinux and Imunify and owns the product concepts that do not yet have a home in an established product line. Ideas come from customer conversations, industry events, telemetry across more than 80,000 servers and the CPO’s strategy; the team’s job is to turn them into something a customer will pay for within a quarter, using AI coding agents throughout.

Prototyping and technical direction.

We evaluate engineers partly on how effectively they work with coding agents, and in the innovation team this is the main lever on speed. As the lead you model and coach it: prompt specificity, review quality on agent-generated code, context provision, iteration and error recovery, and end-to-end task completion. #147748. The Best Stretches to Reduce Quad Pain After a Hard Ski Run, According to a Physical Therapist

The Best Stretches to Reduce Quad Pain After a Hard Ski Run, According to a Physical Therapist

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (719 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes.
  • According to recent reports, even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing—especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer, a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside.
  • The root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that having sore quads after skiing might seem like a side effect reserved for beginners who pizza their way down the slopes. But athletes of all levels can suffer from them.

According to recent reports, even with good form, your quads are the dominant muscle in skiing—especially the lateral quad (vastus lateralis), which is the most active when you turn, James Spencer, a physical therapist in Aspen, Colorado, told Outside. The stronger a skier you are, the harder you can push your quads on the mountain, which means “you can find a way to make them sore, no matter your skiing level,” he explained.

The root cause behind this soreness is the same reason your legs are tender after an arduous trail run or a lower-body weightlifting workout. When you intensely and repeatedly load your quads, you create microscopic tears in the muscle fibers. That damage may sound bad, but it’s actually a good thing: it’s one of the triggers that tells your body to strengthen that muscle, Spencer stated.

It has been revealed that still, the side effects can be unpleasant. As with any bodily injury, the microtears trigger swelling, which increases the pain you feel after exercise and causes that sore sensation, Spencer explains. Officially known as delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS), this feeling sets in after your workout ends and can peak as late as two to three days after. So if you feel fine boarding the shuttle at the end of a long ski day, but find yourself hobbling to the toilet the next morning, DOMS is probably the culprit.

The true cure for DOMS is time. “You really just gotta wait for those [microtears] to heal,” Spencer mentioned. But there’s also something you can do in the interim to ease your pain slightly: quad stretches.

By gently stretching your quads after a hard day on the mountain, you can decrease the intensity of your soreness by flushing out some of the inflammation in your muscles, Spencer remarked. It won’t be a cure-all, but it can help you move and feel better in the short term. Read on for the specific moves Spencer recommends.

You don’t need a ton of quad stretches to find relief. In fact, Spencer notes two are enough. You’ve probably seen these stretches before, and while, sure, they’re not the most exciting, they are simple and effective.

Industry observers note that optional: Do this stretch in a hot tub. The heat may also help reduce feelings of soreness.

The above stretches can be sufficient to help reduce quad soreness, but if you’re looking for more, Spencer also suggests other recovery methods.

Sources indicate that spend a couple of minutes foam rolling your quads, including the front of your thigh (from the knee all the way up to the hip) and the sides to hit the vastus lateralis (basically where your IT band is). Similar to stretching, foam rolling can bring some relief to the quads by reducing swelling in the area.

It has been revealed that another option: hop on a stationary bike and gently cycle your legs for ten to 15 minutes. This easy movement can also reduce soreness by pumping out inflammation from your quads, Spencer mentioned. Just make sure to keep the resistance and your effort level low. “It’s not meant to be a workout,” he said.

Stretches can ease DOMS in the short term, but if you want to prevent intense soreness altogether, strengthening your quads is the ticket.

“If you just build a little strength going into the season, you’re going to be less sore,” Spencer said. And you’re also less likely to get injured, he added.

Exercises such as quad sets, wall sits, and really any squat variation like traditional squats, Bulgarian split squats, and single-leg squats can all strengthen the muscle group.

“The thing I hear all the time is the only way to get ready for skiing is by skiing, and that’s a total lie,” Spencer said. There’s a lot you can do both in the off-season and throughout the winter to prime your body for the demands of skiing, he said. In addition to quad-strengthening exercises, he recommends hamstring, glute, and core moves, plus jumping exercises that train your ability to react to the unexpected.

#147747. What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1230 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Backpacker ↗ Open Full Page

What Does Trail Magic Look Like Around the World? These 5 Stories Show Us

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan).
  • On the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected.
  • That’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The snacks at the hut made Matt's day, despite the mucky conditions (Photo: Matt Jordan).

On the 2024 Highlander UAE, a multi-day 40-mile hike through the Hajar Mountains, I struggled far more than I had expected. The terrain was brutal, with steep descents over sharp, rocky granite tracks along the 6,345-foot Jebel Jais summit. My heavy pack weighed me down, and I could feel every stone beneath my boots. By day three, my two significant toes hurt so much that on one challenging descent, I collapsed and couldn’t take another step.

That’s when a local Emirati man came walking up the trail behind me. He saw that I was struggling and stopped to pull out a roll of tape from his bag. Then, he peeled off my very stinky hiking socks without a second thought, taped up my toes, and bandaged my knees. He even carried my pack for several miles, guiding me down the remaining steep sections.

This stranger had no reason to go out of his way to help me, and I know I could not have finished that day without him. Hikers call this kind of experience “trail magic.” The Appalachian Trail Conservancy defines the term as any instance of finding what you need most when you least expect it; experiencing something rare, extraordinary, or inspiring in nature, or encountering unexpected acts of generosity that restore one’s faith in humanity.

In a recent development, trail magic is often associated with Appalachian Trail history from the early 1980s. However, after my experience in the UAE, I started wondering what it looks like elsewhere. So, here are five stories from other hikers who have experienced trail magic in one form or another around the world.

Sources indicate that matt Jordan, a hiking and backpacking guide with Intrepid Travel, was walking New Zealand’s 1,881-mile Te Araroa Trail southbound in 2023 when he hit the muddy Longwood Forest in Fiordland. After a miserable day of rain and bog, he pushed on toward Turnbull’s Hut, one of the last backcountry huts on that segment. He’d heard that sometimes, free supplies were stored there for hikers passing through. As he approached, he prayed it hadn’t already all been taken by the time he got there.

Recent findings suggest that “Thankfully it hadn’t,” he claims. When he opened the store area, he found a cache of goodies.

“A local man who hikes in supplies, hauls out trash, and maintains the hut about twice a month leaves coolers stocked with beer, soda, and candy bars,” Jordan claims. Excitedly, he grabbed a drink, then promptly slipped in the mud and fell on his backside. After days of awful weather conditions, though, that didn’t stop him from laughing out loud.

According to recent reports, “For me, the gesture was about more than a cold drink. It was a reminder of the generosity of strangers and the sense of community that makes long-distance hikes unforgettable worldwide.”.

Recent findings suggest that meeta Singh Rao, a hiking guide in India, says some of her best trail magic came from shepherds who spend months in the high mountain pastures of the Indian Himalayas. In October 2022, she was leading a trek to Nawali Bugyal in Uttarakhand when the weather turned. Heavy rain began to fall, and strong winds blew. The mules carrying their gear were also lost, and camp was miles away.

It has been revealed that the group came across a shepherd with his flock. He heard where they were headed, and offered them shelter in his channi, a mountain hut made of stone, mud, and plastic sheets. “When rainwater leaked through the roof, he walked out into the downpour to rearrange the plastic so we stayed dry,” states Rao.

Recent findings suggest that when Rao offered to pay, the shepherd gently refused, saying they were his guests. “A couple with so little of their own opened their home to us, giving us a feeling of belonging in the mountains,” she adds.

It has been revealed that kaitlyn Bussell has walked four Caminos. But her second, the 62-mile Camino Inglés in September 2023 through Galicia, was particularly challenging. The rain was constant, few hostels and cafés were open in the fall, and she walked long stretches without seeing another pilgrim.

Sources indicate that on the second day, wet and ready for a break, she ducked into the first bar she found for a café con leche and to charge her phone. When she went to pay, the young woman behind the counter told her the coffee was free and handed her some water, prayer cards and a small Camino keepsake.

Sources indicate that “It was a small thing, but it came at exactly the right moment,” Bussell recalls. “After days of rain, it lifted my spirits and made me realize that this pilgrimage is as much about the people you meet as it is the miles you walk.”.

On Japan’s Shikoku 88 Temples Pilgrimage route, Lauren Roerick and her brother were leaving one of the temples when she spotted a sign offering matcha tea ceremonies for pilgrims. They initially walked away unsure whether they would be intruding but returned and decided to try it anyway.

“A Japanese man welcomed us inside where two women in kimonos were preparing and serving matcha under his instruction,” adds Roerick. “To make us feel welcome, he called a friend and had her on speakerphone, translating the whole ceremony from Japanese into English.” Lauren and her brother learned about the tradition, tried making tea themselves, and ate small Japanese sweets.

“It was proof that trail magic isn’t always a bottle of water or a helping hand,” indicates Roerick. “Sometimes a stranger opens his door, works around a language barrier, and shares a bit of culture with people passing through.”.

On a windy hike to Matterhorn Base Camp, Libera Pagano, tour director with EF Adventures, noticed an older woman struggling. The altitude made her dizzy, her legs were shaking, and her friend had walked far ahead. “I offered to sit with the woman while she rested behind a large rock and we started chatting,” says Pagano.

Industry observers note that that’s when Pagano learned it was the woman’s 86th birthday, and the hike was a present she’d given herself. They stayed together, and when the woman felt ready, they walked slowly until they caught up with her companion. When the group met back at basecamp, the woman told Pagano that without her help, she would never have made it to the summit.

“I thought nothing of what I had done,” says Pagano. “But for that woman, it was the difference between giving up and fulfilling her birthday wish.”.

Industry observers note that I never learned the name of the man who bandaged my toes in the Hajar Mountains, and I probably never will. But I think about him whenever I struggle on a trail or see another hiker limping.

Industry observers note that all these stories have one thing in common—human compassion. Sometimes that is stopping to help a stranger in need, sharing what little you have, or leaving a cache of supplies for a hiker you’ll probably never meet. These gestures don’t have to be grand or cost much, but they can make an enormous difference and are an easy thing to pay forward so everyone experiences a little magic outdoors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground.
  • “On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” indicates Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete.
  • In a recent development, explosive strength can be trained, though.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hills don’t just feel hard. Tackling steep slopes takes way more energy than walking or running at the same pace on flat ground: In fact, you burn roughly 44 percent more calories per hour walking up a 5 percent incline than on flat ground. If you’ve got that one hiking buddy who seems to power up the hills while you’re huffing and puffing, the reason isn’t just that they’re fit. It’s that they’ve built up power—specifically explosive strength, which is fitness jargon for their ability to quickly muster the strength they’ve built. Explosive strength is the same stuff you use when you jump, bound, or push yourself up a steep step.

“On every uphill stride … the first thing that happens is a very, very sharp kind of eccentric stretching load on the leg as you step up, and then you need a much higher power spike to actually get the body moving,” indicates Alex Viada, head coach at Complete Human Performance, and author of The Ultimate Hybrid Athlete. “If you don’t have the ability to hit those little power spikes over and over and over again, that’s a much greater determinant of uphill performance.”.

In a recent development, explosive strength can be trained, though. In a small 2011 study of women in their 60s and 70s published in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity, one group was assigned to lift weights in a way that would build explosive strength. After 12 weeks, those women climbed stairs 17 percent faster than they did at the beginning of the study.

“Uphills are hard, and they’re hard for everyone,” says Mike Aidala, coach and owner of The Offense, a gym and mindset coaching business in Boulder, CO. He says that approaching your training with a goal of getting stronger, rather than faster, can help build uphill power.

Here’s a mental intent method from the study that can make every exercise build more explosive strength, and six specific exercises for building explosive, uphill strength from Viada, Aidala, and Rose Wetzel, a certified personal trainer and pro Spartan racer with multiple world championship podium finishes.

Sources indicate that explosive exercises are usually those where your body leaves the floor (like squat jumps or box jumps) or a weight leaves your hands (like medicine ball throws). But you can achieve the same benefit by performing the concentric phase—the “lift” phase—of any exercise with explosive intent. That’s how the elderly participants in the Journal of Aging and Physical Activity study built power. On each repetition of machine exercises, they did the eccentric—or “lowering”—portion of the lift at a controlled pace, and then they pushed the weight up in an explosive manner.

Recent findings suggest that lifting weights in this way gives a two-way boost to your uphill performance. Not only does it build power in the “push” portion of each lift, but lowering weights slowly and under control increases the strength of your tendons.

“When we train our tendons, we’re able to be more explosive,” notes Wetzel. Stronger tendons, she says, “help with the body’s ability to spring off the ground, to explode off with all that strength.”.

According to recent reports, you can use this method with almost every strength exercise you do, states Viada. His recommendation: Start with a few sets of each exercise with explosive intent, and then move into your “regular” sets of the move. During the explosive sets, he says, don’t use as much weight as you will in the later, “normal” sets.

According to recent reports, for a starting weight, Viada suggests subtracting 25 percent from the maximum weight with which you could normally perform 10 reps. For example, if you regularly do 10 leg presses with 200 pounds, perform your explosive reps with 150 pounds.

Sources indicate that in addition to using a lower weight, Viada also recommends doing fewer repetitions in each set. While you could probably do this weight for 15 or more repetitions, start with a handful, and make sure each one is done with maximum explosive intention.

“The only thing that matters is that they’re explosive and they’re fast,” he states. “So when you go to the bottom of the movement, think about suddenly trying to push the bar or sled up through a wall. Pretend you’re trying to smash [the weight] up through the ceiling.”.

Do a few sets in this way for each move, then move to your normal, longer sets with your regular weights.

Our experts recommend these six moves to become more explosive and more stable as you trek or run uphill—they’re moves the coaches have used to train clients to climb 14ers, and that Wetzel herself has used to vault her way to multiple obstacle course race podiums.

Sources indicate that the first four exercises can be done anywhere, including as part of a run or hike warmup. For the last two, you’ll need some gym equipment.

According to recent reports, these jumps let you practice exploding, but also train your knee not to wobble on each step. Not only will a stable knee help prevent injuries when you’re thrown off-kilter on the trail, but will prevent you from losing energy that could be used to propel you forward.

Industry observers note that do one set of 10 jumps per leg three to four times per week. Over time, try to minimize wobbling, and then increase the distance of your jumps.

Similar to the previous exercise, these jumps incorporate side-to-side movement. Don’t rush through them, Aidala claims. Land, get stable, take a beat, then repeat.

Do 10 jumps in each direction on each leg. Perform these three to four times per week.

These aren’t the plodding high knees you’re used to, Wetzel says.

It has been revealed that “When I do these drills, it’s for a very short amount of time, and I do them for power,” she states. “I’m not doing high knees like someone might do for 30 seconds to get their heart rate up … it’s like six to eight seconds of hot potato, hot potato, hot potato, and then catch my breath for 30 seconds.”.

You can do these before every run or hike, or as a warmup before any workout.

Sources indicate that this move, Wetzel indicates, helps you to feel like you can spring off with each step up a hill. Unlike a longer jumping lunge, she does these mini lunges as swiftly as possible, keeping the movement “fierce, short, and explosive.” Instead of dropping into a full lunge, bend your knees only slightly, with your feet moving front to back almost like you’re cross-country skiing while jumping slightly.

Do a few sets of 16 reps before every run, hike, or gym workout.

Sources indicate that “Uphill running starts from the hips,” Viada notes. “And with Bulgarian split squat hops, when you start that explosiveness from the bottom, you’ll explosively engage those hips like nothing else.”.

It has been revealed that this takes one of the most dreaded moves in the gym and adds an explosive element, with the front foot leaving the ground on each repetition. Your foot doesn’t need to come way off the ground, though, Viada says. An inch or so is great. Since it’s already a tough move, he recommends using a light weight, or no weight at all.

Perform three to four sets of four to five hops per leg, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these two to three times per week.

When lifting with explosive intent, coaches often recommend that you “explode out of the hole,” or the bottom of the move. With the Anderson squat, you start in the hole using a squat rack, pressing the bar off pins so you can focus even more on the powerful concentric portion of the lift.

Sources indicate that don’t set the stops on the rack too low, Viada says. Aim so that when you get under the bar, your knees are bent 90 degrees, mimicking the angles you’ll need to hike uphill with power.

Recent findings suggest that perform three to four sets of four to five squats, focusing on explosiveness in each rep. Do these one to two times per week.

#147742. Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1005 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Outsideonline ↗ Open Full Page

Adrian Ballinger Is Returning to Mount Everest’s South Side. Here’s Why.

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ballinger, founder of Alpenglow Expeditions, is a veteran of Mount Everest climbing (Photo: Griffinf Mims).
  • For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.
  • Recent findings suggest that in interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste, and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ballinger, founder of Alpenglow Expeditions, is a veteran of Mount Everest climbing (Photo: Griffinf Mims).

For more than a decade, American expedition leader Adrian Ballinger swore off guiding climbers up Mount Everest’s popular South Col route in Nepal.

Recent findings suggest that in interviews, Ballinger noted the crowds, the trash, the ever-present problem with human waste, and the frequency of rescues and deaths along the route. Atop his list of concerns, however, was the deadly Khumbu Icefall, the site of avalanches and dangerous crumbling seracs. Every spring, Sherpa porters and guides must make dozens of trips through the crumbling glacier to ferry food, tents, and oxygen to higher camps.

“If you run 20 trips on Everest over the next 20 years and hire 15 to 20 Sherpas each year, you’re putting a lot of people’s lives in danger,” Ballinger told Outside in a 2023 interview. “We don’t feel that we can run an ethical expedition from the south side.”.

Ballinger’s company, Alpenglow Expeditions, led a handful of trips to Everest’s south side in the aughts. But starting in 2014, Alpenglow exclusively led Everest trips from the mountain’s northern side in Tibet, which is controlled by China.

It has been revealed that now, Ballinger is taking steps to return to Everest’s southern side. In a recent interview, he told Outside that his three-year strategy for Alpenglow is to lead trips up Everest from both Tibet and Nepal concurrently.

“Even though we still think the north side of Everest is better for our clients, we are considering the south side as a backup,” Ballinger said. “And ultimately, we hope to be able to run trips on both sides of the mountain, provided we get the approvals that we expect.”.

Returning to Nepal gives Alpenglow a backup initiative in case China closes the peak to climbers, Ballinger said.

Recent findings suggest that climbers tackling Everest from the northern side of the China-Nepal border enjoy a few advantages, namely smaller crowds and a Base Camp accessible by vehicles. But the Chinese government’s repeated decision to close Everest with little warning has stymied expedition leaders. In 2008, China closed Everest just weeks before the climbing season to allow the Olympic torch relay to ascend the peak.

Since 2016, China has shuttered Everest five additional times. It closed the peak in 2020 due to the Covid pandemic, and kept Everest off-limits through the 2023 season. Ballinger returned the following year with an expedition to the top.

“We had incredible seasons on Everest in 2024 and 2025, some of the best of my life,” Ballinger stated. “It was uncrowded, we had great support from the Chinese, and it was totally open.”.

In a recent development, in 2026, Ballinger and other guides were preparing for another successful season on Everest’s north side when China abruptly canceled the season in early March. The decision came painfully late in the season. Expedition operators had already promised paychecks to guides and mountain workers. And climbers usually arrive at Base Camps in China and Nepal in mid-April.

“We took the financial losses and did the right thing,” Ballinger said. “We paid our Sherpas and our guides and our workers who waited until the end. We ate that cost.”.

Sources indicate that ballinger mentioned he then gave his climbing clients refunds or deferrals to the 2027 season. One-third accepted deferrals to 2027, while two-thirds booked with other outfitters in Nepal in 2026, he said. Alpenglow helped its clients find expeditions to join on Everest’s south side for the 2026 season.

It has been revealed that “Financially it’s not easy,” Ballinger stated. “It definitely sucks, but we want the best for our clients.”.

Operating in both Nepal and Tibet, however, would allow Alpenglow to shift clients from one side of the peak to the other in the instance of a closure.

“Between 2007 and this year—that’s 20 seasons—we’ve had to cancel six times,” he mentioned. “In those years there’s a lot of stress.”.

According to recent reports, ballinger cited the rapid introduction of cargo-carrying drones on Everest’s south side as another reason for his decision to return. In 2026, a manufacturer called Airlift Technologies began ferrying gear and supplies from Base Camp at 17,500 feet over the Khumbu Icefall up to Camp I at 19,900 feet via heavy-duty cargo drones.

Alpenglow’s lead guide, Esteban “Topo” Mena, spent time at the Nepali Base Camp in 2026 to watch the business grow.

Industry observers note that “We sent Topo to check out the scene and see if he thought the experimentation that’s going on with drone technology had a meaningful impact,” Ballinger said. “We think we can replace all of our Sherpa carries through the Khumbu Icefall with drones.”.

It has been revealed that each drone delivery to Camp I eliminates a human trip through the Khumbu Icefall. In 2026, several Everest outfitters relied heavily on Airlift Technologies’ drone service to transport gear above Base Camp.

The drone business grew out of two seasons of testing. Starting in 2024, Nepali drone companies began completing test flights of heavy-duty cargo drones amid the thin air at Everest Base Camp. In 2025, drone pilots successfully flew an oxygen canister and bags of gear from Base Camp to Camp I, proving the potential for a drone business.

The drone business is not without its problems. In 2026, the Nepali government grounded Airlift Technologies’ drones for four days without explanation.

Piloting a cargo drone over the Khumbu Icefall requires skill and technological innovation. One pilot at Base Camp controls the drone at takeoff. But when the craft reaches a specific elevation, a second pilot at Camp I takes over control, navigating the craft past towers of ice and sheer rock walls to land it on the upper flanks of the Khumbu Glacier.

“We see it as a really exciting change,” Ballinger said. “We’ve been talking for years now about what would allow the icefall to become manageable in the long term. We think drones are a stepping stone in that direction.”.

A Basset Hound Demonstrated Up Alone at a Hiking Area—and Kicked Off a Lifesaving Rescue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (767 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • (Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).
  • Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Upcoming York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.
  • Recent findings suggest that the day prior, Becky indicated up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: NYS Department of Environmental Conservation).

Rescuers saved a 69-year-old hiker in Upcoming York’s Adirondack Mountains on November 13 thanks to a swift search effort—and a Basset Hound named Becky.

Recent findings suggest that the day prior, Becky indicated up at the base of Whiteface Mountain without her owner. Staff immediately recognized the dog. They knew her owner suffered from dementia, and the fact that he wasn’t with Becky concerned them. They contacted 911 to report the owner missing.

According to recent reports, fresh York State police officers responded and located the hiker’s car at a nearby trailhead. According to Syracuse.com, several officers searched the trails in the immediate area and a branch of the Ausable River. However, they found nothing. Four forest rangers joined the effort, deploying a drone and bloodhound to the area.

But time wasn’t on their side. Night fell without any sign of the lost hiker, and organizers called off the search with intends to resume it in the morning. According to the Department of Environmental Conservation (DEC), temperatures on the night of Thursday, November 12, dropped to between 25 and 30 degrees around Whiteface Mountain.

According to recent reports, when the sun rose, the search continued with even more resources and rescuers. Fourteen rangers and state police aviation began combing Whiteface Mountain. Using cell phone data, police pinpointed the hiker’s phone; however, when searchers located it, they discovered the phone abandoned along with the hiker’s backpack.

Industry observers note that finally, around 10 a.m., the searchers got lucky. A hunter in the area heard someone scream in the woods. A ranger responded to sweep the area and located the missing hiker in an open meadow.

“This gentleman didn’t have shoes on when we found him in the morning, or mittens or gloves,” Charlie Foutch, a ranger who had been part of the search, told Syracuse.com. “Sometimes when you keep moving in that situation, you generate enough heat to do OK, and he was still alive.”.

Foutch stated that’s largely also thanks to Becky.

In a recent development, “It definitely would have been much harder to find him [without her]. He may not have survived the rest of the day, and probably not another night,” Foutch stated. “The dog definitely contributed to him being saved so rapidly.”.

The hiker’s hands and feet were severely frostbitten and required immediate medical attention. A helicopter airlifted him to a nearby hospital.

According to recent reports, people with Alzheimer’s or other types of dementia are common subjects of wilderness searches. In an interview with the Fisher Center for Alzheimer’s Research Foundation, Kimberly Kelly, an international rescue specialist, said there are around 125,000 SAR operations involving missing Alzheimer’s subjects every year—and that number is on the rise.

It has been revealed that “In most categories, SAR missions are going down, or declining, for a variety of reasons,” Kelly states. “However, SAR missions for the missing at-risk, wandering Alzheimer’s patients are increasing dramatically, and that is expected to continue to increase exponentially over the coming years.”.

Industry observers note that wes Cooper is a volunteer field leader with Seattle Mountain Rescue (SMR). He told Backpacker that roughly a third of SMR’s search operations involve individuals with dementia or Alzheimers. Most occur in urban settings, but he notes SMR has responded to this type of rescue in the wilderness as well.

“Say it’s the middle of the night and we need to try to find somebody quickly, or if it’s turning into a multi-day mission with a larger SAR planning strategy, we will not only deploy ground teams to canvas neighborhoods, the backcountry trails, or even off-trail, but we’ll throw technology at the search, too.”.

According to recent reports, he indicates e-bikes not only expand their reach, but also increase response times and deployment speed. Drones help them scan larger areas from above. And they even use algorithms that predict how far someone might have wandered, based on how long they’ve been missing.

Urgency is particularly crucial in these cases, Cooper notes. Research shows that subjects with Alzheimer’s whom rescuers are unable to find within 24 hours have a 46 percent mortality rate. In areas like the Adirondacks, when terrain and weather are factored in, that number can be much higher.

That’s why Cooper says, “Don’t hesitate to call 911 and get the agencies going,” as Whiteface Mountain staff did in the case of Becky’s owner. It’s better to get help fast, even if you find the lost person close to home, rather than trying to look for them yourself and letting valuable time slip away.

#147739. 6 Underrated Mountain Towns to Visit This Winter
