6 Underrated Mountain Towns to Visit This Winter

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These are the mountain towns that dominate our winter daydreams.
  • It has been revealed that I cover mountain towns for Outside, and every year I start plotting out my own winter getaways right about now.
  • A couple of these towns are my longtime favorites, while others are still on my “must-go” list.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You know the big names. Jackson, Wyoming. Stowe, Vermont. Telluride, Colorado. These are the mountain towns that dominate our winter daydreams. The famous ski towns that make us consider taking a sabbatical, buying a van, and living the Aspen Extreme dream for three months in the heart of winter. But there are other winter adventure spots that deserve the spotlight.

It has been revealed that I cover mountain towns for Outside, and every year I start plotting out my own winter getaways right about now. Sure, I enjoy hitting up established destinations like Park City as much as the next skier, but the towns on this list get me excited because they fly under the radar. They don’t receive a ton of hype, but they have access to amazing powder stashes, lengthy trail systems, and resort lines that are far shorter than their better-known counterparts’.

A couple of these towns are my longtime favorites, while others are still on my “must-go” list. Here are six often overlooked winter mountain towns that you need to visit once the snow starts to gather.

A legitimate winter town in the South? Yes indeed. Boone is a vibrant college town that grows when Appalachian State’s roughly 20,000 students are in session. It has all of the hallmarks of a fun-loving mountain town, with plenty of dive bars and burrito joints to keep you satiated. But it also sits in North Carolina’s High Country, surrounded by 5,000- and 6,000-foot mountains, which get some of the heaviest snowfalls in the region. There are three ski resorts within 30 minutes of downtown and some of the most consistent cross-country skiing in the South on a series of 6,000-foot peaks near the Tennessee border.

Winter Adventures: You have three downhill resorts to choose from, but Beech Mountain Resort is the highest ski resort in eastern North America, with a summit elevation of 5,506 feet. It also has a bar, the 5506′ Skybar, at the top of the mountain and its own brewery in the base village. As for the terrain, the mountain has 95 acres and just over 800 feet of drop, so you’ll need to do laps to get in your vert. But the terrain park gets better every year, and skiers can usually count on about 80 inches of snow every winter. Full-day adult lift tickets start at $57 on weekdays.

In a recent development, but the best winter adventure near Boone is cross-country skiing Roan Mountain, a high ridge that tops out at 6,285 feet, gets heavy snowfall, and has a variety of terrain to ski, from high-elevation grassy balds to singletrack through rhododendron tunnels. The only catch is you’ll need to bring your own skis, as rentals are scarce in the South. Start at Carver’s Gap and head up the gated Forest Service road, which climbs gradually for about two miles to the Rhododendron Gardens. You’ll get long-range views in both directions and the option to hop onto more challenging trails that branch off the road.

Duluth is a longtime shipping and industrial city at the western tip of Lake Superior that has found upcoming life as an adventure hub, with a world-class mountain bike trail system traversing the hills on the edge of downtown. But the city’s location in northern Minnesota means winter hits the city hard. Duluth gets about 86 inches of lake-effect snow each winter, and that snow sticks around because high temperatures stay below freezing on more than 100 days a year. The constant cold temps are ideal for ice climbing, and the consistent snow and cornucopia of mountain bike trails mean Duluth becomes a fat-biking and cross-country ski mecca during winter.

Need more reasons to visit? How about downhill skiing at nearby Spirit Mountain, which has 175 acres of terrain with 700 feet of vertical drop.

Winter Adventures: Northern Minnesota has a legitimate ski culture, and Spirit Mountain has some of the best blue cruisers in the Midwest, many of which have long-range views of downtown Duluth and Lake Superior. The mountain also has two terrain parks, one for beginners looking to progress and one for shredders looking to send it. There’s a welcoming uphill policy for anyone who wants to earn their turns on touring gear, too. Adult tickets start at $83.

But Duluth is a bike town, and when the snow falls that means it’s time to roll out the fat tires. Many sections of the Duluth Traverse, an epic 40-mile-long route that runs from one side of the city to the other, are groomed for fat bikes in the winter. The machine-built trails in Mission Creek, with their berms and rollers, are particularly fun with a layer of packed snow. Local outfitter Day Tripper offers guided fat-bike tours and rentals.

In a recent development, newly introduced England got hammered with snow last winter, with the highest elevations in the mountains getting more than 200 inches of snow, and the tiny town of Jackson was poised to make the most of it. This picture-perfect village, which comes complete with a general store and covered bridge, sits on the edge of White Mountain National Forest with fast access to downhill skiing at Black Mountain and roughly 90 miles of cross-country ski trails scattered throughout the valley.

Jackson doesn’t have the cachet of some other ski towns in Latest England, but American ski culture got an early boost here when Black Mountain opened in 1935, making it one of the first lift operations in the country. And that culture is still thriving. Case in point: check out Friday Night Lights, a weekly uphill party where skiers put on headlamps and ski to the top of the mountain en masse.

Winter Adventures: The Jackson Ski Touring Foundation grooms and maintains about 150 kilometers of trails, all surrounding a touring center with rentals and lessons. The trails traverse the community throughout three consecutive river valleys over 60 square miles. You’ll get views of Mount Washington from open meadows, tight singletrack through woods, and even the chance to hit trailside restaurants in certain spots. Day passes start at $29.

According to recent reports, no trip to Jackson is complete without some laps at Black Mountain, a proudly independent ski resort with 140 acres of glades, narrow groomers, and nonexistent lift lines. You’ll get 1,100 feet of vertical drop, with the steepest terrain at the summit, and a lively pub (the Shovel Handle Pub) at the base of the mountain for après-ski activities. Adult lift tickets start at $49.

Pagosa Springs and the surrounding area suffered a flood this fall, but the town and Wolf Creek are open and actively asking for travelers to visit this winter as tourism is integral to their economy. When you visit, keep in mind that locals and businesses might still be dealing with impacts from the flood. Your money helps, but so does your patience and understanding.

It has been revealed that the San Juan Mountains are home to some of Colorado’s most iconic mountain towns and most well-regarded ski slopes, but most skiers don’t explore the region beyond Telluride and Silverton. Dig deeper into the mountains of southwest Colorado and you’ll find tiny Pagosa Springs, which sits on the banks of the San Juan River. The hamlet is best known for its geothermal springs, but the mountains surrounding this hot-water hub are even more enticing. Pagosa Springs is 23 miles from Wolf Creek Ski Area, which is known as one of the snowiest mountains in Colorado, pulling down an average of 430 inches of snow every winter.

Sources indicate that want more variety? Summer waterfalls turn into ice-climbing playgrounds when the temperature drops, and the local Nordic club grooms more than 50 kilometers of skate and classic ski trails near town.

Industry observers note that winter Adventures: Forget the champagne huts and concierge service you find at many ski resorts these days. Wolf Creek is a no-frills operation that’s all about the snow and the terrain, with 430 inches of annual snowfall that blanket wide groomers and steep trees. OK, a lot of trees. Wolf Creek has a significant amount of expert terrain, which plays out in a series of steep bowls at the top of the resort and seemingly endless glades all over the mountain. And you won’t have to take out a loan to fund this trip; full-day adult lift tickets at Wolf Creek are right at $110.

The 50 kilometers of cross-country ski trails begin in town, with a mile-long loop inside the town park that’s perfect for beginners. But this is a great chance to dip a toe into fat biking. There’s an 8.5-mile loop that’s groomed for fat bikes when snow allows, winding through a ponderosa pine forest. Pagosa Mountain Sport rents cross-country skis and fat bikes.

Sources indicate that park City, Salt Lake City…these are the ski towns that get the press, but Ogden? Ogden doesn’t typically make the list. But it should. This historic city, which was the first permanent settlement by people of European descent in the state of Utah, sits between the Great Salt Lake and the Wasatch Mountains, just 40 minutes north of Salt Lake City, but seemingly a world apart. Downtown Ogden is anchored by 25th Street, a historic main street with upscale Wild West charm, while three ski resorts known for deep powder are less than 30 minutes away. Powder Mountain anchors the trio, with more than 8,000 acres of terrain, but Snowbasin is continually ranked one of the best ski resorts in the country by Ski magazine and the smaller Nordic Valley has a local-hill vibe complete with night skiing. Bonus: You don’t have to fight Salt Lake City’s notorious canyon traffic to make your turns.

According to recent reports, winter Adventures: You’re here to ski, so get after it at Powder Mountain, the largest ski resort in the Lower 48. Powder has 2,800 acres of lift-served terrain with more than 2,000 feet of vertical drop, but the real gem here is Powder’s sidecountry. Head through the Powder Country or Woody’s World entrance gates from the lift-served side of the mountain and you’ll have 1,200 acres of ungroomed, off-piste action at your ski tips. The best part? A shuttle bus picks you up at the bottom of your line and takes you back to the front of the mountain, so there’s no boot-packing involved. Adult lift tickets start at $99.

It has been revealed that you might also want to try your hand at sledding AKA snowmobiling while you’re in Ogden. The Monte Cristo area, east of the Ogden Valley, has some of the best snowmobile terrain in the state, including a 63-mile groomed loop that’s perfect for beginners and has long-range views of the Ogden Valley. Club Rec North offers tours and rentals next to the trailhead. Tours with rentals start at $229.

This former gold-mining post in the North Cascades really leans into its historic roots, with a downtown that’s lined with Old West-style false fronts and wooden boardwalks. And that western heritage is still alive and well. A number of outfitters offer horseback adventures and the annual Ride to Rendezvous, a four-day horse-packing trip complete with a wagon train that rolls into town for Winthrop’s ’49er Days parade. But make no mistake, Winthrop has found latest life as a ski town. Well, a skinny-ski town. The Methow Valley surrounding Winthrop has one of the most extensive cross-country trail networks in the country with more than 120 miles of groomed, marked and maintained paths to explore.

Looking for a cozy vibe for the whole family? Take a spin around Winthrop Rink, the town’s outdoor ice-skating rink that serves as the social hub for the season.

In a recent development, winter Adventures: If you’re spending time in Winthrop, then you’re here to ski the Methow Trails. With more than 120 miles of obsessively groomed paths, there is something for everyone in this valley. Want to ski from lodge to lodge? That’s an option. Want a pretty loop around a lake? No problem. Want to spend the day climbing an obscene amount of vertical? They have you covered. The Methow Trails organization runs clinics and camps all season if you want to improve your kick-and-glide form or maybe try your hand at biathlon. Day passes start at $32.

Loup Loup Ski Bowl is a lift-served mountain with 300 acres that’s operated by a nonprofit. There are 10 runs with 1,240 vertical feet of drop. You’ll find beginner trails and expert trails that drop from the top of the mountain and a very welcoming uphill ski culture if you want to earn your turns. And you’ve got to check out the Ski Bowl’s luge course, where you guide an old-school sled down groomed trails. Adult lift tickets start at $80.

Graham Averill is Outside magazine’s national parks columnist. He loves warm-weather adventures, but he gets absolutely giddy when ski season approaches, and writing articles like this helps him initiative his ski trips.

Hike of the Week: Explore the Dramatic—and Threatened—Significant Bend on This Desert Peak

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (696 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Backpacker

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S.
  • Recent findings suggest that nine years later, Substantial Bend is still beautiful.
  • One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

(Photo: kellyvandellen/Getty Images).

The first time I visited Santa Elena Canyon, the gorge in Big Bend National Park that straddles the border between the U.S. and Mexico, I was amazed not just at how beautiful it was, but how peaceful. The buff and black-streaked limestone walls soared 1,500 feet over the water, the afternoon sun streaming through the gap. The river was running low and slow, trickling over the mud and rocks, no more than knee deep. I rolled up my pant legs and waded into the water, toward that invisible line in the middle of the river that split two countries.

Recent findings suggest that nine years later, Substantial Bend is still beautiful. Covering an area bigger than Rhode Island, this stretch of West Texas desert is home to some of the state’s most moving scenery, from river canyons to rocky peaks, with animal and plant life to match. Hikers willing to put in the work on the area’s rugged trails may spot javelinas rooting in the undergrowth or nocturnal, raccoon-like ringtails climbing up the cliffs and trees of the Chisos Mountains; they’ll see prickly pear cactus and ocotillo, a spindly, Seussian shrub equipped with vicious spines, growing wild in the desert flats. (That border, however, may soon be far more concrete. Read on for more on that.).

One of the best ways to see it today is the hike up Emory Peak. At 7,825 feet, Emory is the highest point in Substantial Bend and the Chisos, and enjoys commanding views of the terrain for miles around. Getting there, however, takes some muscle: The rough, 9.7-mile hike to the top ascends singletrack and rock stairs through oak, piñon, and juniper forest before ending with a final, dramatic scramble to the peak’s exposed summit. November, when summer’s broiling temperatures finally cool down, is an ideal time to hike it. (Note: There is no water at all along the Emory Peak Trail, and the NPS suggests hikers carry at least one liter per person per hour.).

It has been revealed that the round trip takes about 6 to 8 hours, and you’ll want to leave some time to relax afterward. Santa Elena Canyon’s picnic area is an ideal spot for an early dinner, and cap off the night at the park’s free riverside hot springs. (Due to recent flood damage, reaching both of these highlights is currently harder than usual. The paved road between Cottonwood Campground and Santa Elena is closed at the time of writing; drivers with a true 4-wheel drive vehicle and high clearance can get there on Old Maverick Road. Due to another closure, getting to the hot springs requires a 4-mile round-trip, relatively flat hike along a gravel road. Consider it part of the adventure.).

Industry observers note that starting at the Chisos Basin Visitors Center, take the Laguna Meadows trail for about a third of a mile to a fork, where you’ll hang a left on the Pinnacles Trail. Follow it as it steadily climbs, traversing desert flats and rocky slopes with the sheer top of Emory looming in the background. After another 3.4 miles, the trail reaches a saddle below the top of the peak. Continue on the Emory Peak Trail for another 1.5 miles, then tackle a final, somewhat exposed 30-foot scramble to the top of the mountain and 360-degree views of the park below. Retrace your steps to the trailhead, or break up the hike by reserving one of the Pinnacles campsites ahead of your trip.

According to recent reports, in an 8-1 decision on November 9, the Supreme Court approved a request by the Trump administration to resume construction of a border wall through Massive Bend, ruling against plaintiffs who had argued that the barrier would decimate rare plant species and cut off migratory routes for animals, and that it risked damaging ancient rock art and Native heritage sites. In Santa Elena Canyon itself, the Department of Homeland Security plans to install vehicle barriers and surveillance infrastructure and clear patrol roads through the area. Conservation groups and state officials like Governor-Elect Gina Hinojosa say they’ll continue to push to end construction in the park.

Your Lower Back Is Probably Working Too Hard. Do These 5 Yoga Moves to Strengthen the Mid-Back.

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1117 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If you’re seeking ways to strengthen your back, chances are you won’t find a lot of solutions for how to strengthen your mid-back.
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to strength training and your back, almost everyone talks about avoiding lower back strain or correcting tech neck.
  • According to recent reports, and that’s a shame.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you’re seeking ways to strengthen your back, chances are you won’t find a lot of solutions for how to strengthen your mid-back. Yoga teacher and certified personal trainer Amber Sayer, who works with desk workers as well as competitive athletes, explains why the missing mid-back component is so essential and how to effectively strengthen it.

Sources indicate that when it comes to strength training and your back, almost everyone talks about avoiding lower back strain or correcting tech neck. But there isn’t much information about how to strengthen and improve endurance in the muscles of the mid-back.

According to recent reports, and that’s a shame. This overlooked part of the body not only contributes to your ease of posture and movement during everyday life, but it also ensures that all of the muscles in your back can work together effectively. Basically, when any part of the back is underutilized, it creates more work for the other parts. Practicing exercises that challenge and build endurance in your mid-back supports functional back strength throughout the spine and helps minimize the risk of forcing the muscles in the lower back to overcompensate. Think of your mid-back muscles as one of those things you don’t tend to think about until there’s a problem.

These muscles attach to the thoracic spine and include the middle and lower trapezius, rhomboids, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, and serratus posterior. You’ve probably already been practicing yoga poses or other exercises that strengthen the muscles in the mid-back in various ways without realizing it.

But when you become more intentional about including the following poses, you ensure that you target the various muscles that, collaboratively, strengthen your entire back.

Rather than practicing the entire list of yoga poses all at once, incorporate a couple into your workout routine, occasionally changing up which ones you explore.

Or try a single pose as a one-off whenever you could use a respite from sitting and staring at your screen.

In a recent development, this beginner-friendly pose is your starting point as you’re learning to strengthen the mid-back muscles. Because Sphinx Pose (Salamba Bhujangasana) props you on your forearms to create the backbend, it can be almost entirely passive for the back muscles. But there are a few subtle actions you can take that engage the mid-back in significant yet non-intense ways.

Industry observers note that lie on your belly with your forehead on the mat and your legs straight behind you, hip-distance apart, with the tops of your feet on the mat. Bring your palms and forearms to the mat with your elbows beneath or slightly in front of your shoulders. Actively press down through your forearms to lift your chest off the mat. Draw your shoulder blades down and away from your ears and toward the middle of your back. And the crucial part for your mid-back is to keep your forearms still but feel as if you’re dragging your elbows toward your hips. Keep that action as you stay here for several breaths.

If the backbend feels too intense, inch your forearms slightly in front of you to lessen how much your chest is lifted from the mat.

In a recent development, this backbend asks you to lift your chest off the mat by pressing your palms to the mat. But when you hover your hands in Cobra Pose (Bhujangasana), you rely exclusively on your mid-back and core muscles to create the shape. The point isn’t how far you lift yourself off the mat. It’s that you create any lift at all.

Start lying on your belly with your palms beneath your shoulders. Start with your palms pressing into the mat and lift your chest. Then press the tops of your feet into the mat and engage your mid-back muscles to lift your chest any amount off the mat. To intensify the workload on your mid-back muscles, lift your palms an inch or two above the mat and continue to hover them. You can also bring your arms straight out from your shoulders like the letter T, and then turn your thumbs toward the ceiling to increase the strengthening potential for the trapezius.

According to recent reports, this shape asks you to actively lift your upper and lower body off the mat, which enlists the mid-back muscles as you counteract gravity. It effectively strengthens not only the mid-back but the entire back body, including the upper and lower back, glutes, and hamstrings. Locust Pose (Salabhasana) is not easy, but it is one of the best back-strengthening yoga poses that exist.

Start lying on your belly with your arms at your sides, palms facing down. Press down through the fronts of the hips and start to lift your upper and lower body off the mat, drawing the shoulder blades toward each other. Lift only as much as you can. Interlace your fingers behind your back and reach your knuckles toward the wall behind you.

Industry observers note that this pose is commonly thought of as a quad-strengthening yoga pose, as that’s usually where you feel the burn. But leaning forward in Chair Pose (Utkatasana) without completely collapsing forward and reaching your arms overhead also challenges—and strengthens—the muscles of the mid-back. Specifically, the lower trapezius and erector spinae.

From standing, bring your significant toes to touch or keep them hip-distance apart. Bend your knees and sit your hips partly back, as if you’re about to sit in a chair. Lean your chest slightly forward and reach your arms alongside your ears. Draw your shoulders away from your ears to strengthen the trapezius and rhomboids.

To intensify the challenge for your mid-back, take any of the following arm variations:.

Recent findings suggest that this Warrior pose tends to be less common than Warrior 1 or 2 when it comes to most yoga strength routines, yet it is an unsung hero in terms of strengthening not only the legs but most of the muscles in your body. The trick for targeting the mid-back muscles is to reach your straightened arms in front of you with your torso in Warrior 3 (Virabhadrasana III).

Recent findings suggest that from standing with your hands on your hips or at your chest, shift your weight into one foot and slowly start to lean forward as you lift the other foot and reach it toward the wall behind you. Slowly reach your arms straight ahead, with your arms alongside your ears. Alternatively, you can reach them alongside your body, with your fingertips reaching toward the back wall, in what’s commonly referred to as airplane arms. Imagine actively lifting your straightened arms up toward the ceiling.

4 Heritage Adventure Motorcycles for Wherever the Pavement Ends

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1168 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The air drops five degrees as soon as I start heading uphill on Angeles Crest.
  • At 5,300 feet, across from Charlton Flat, I find what I’m looking for: a faded stop sign, a faded five mph sign, then a crisp yellow square: STREET LEGAL ONLY.
  • These bikes were made for exactly this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The air drops five degrees as soon as I start heading uphill on Angeles Crest. A road I’ve motorcycled hundreds of times, but it always feels like it could lead somewhere unexpected. A yellow diamond sign says 44 miles of curves ahead. Spanish broom flickers yellow in the breeze and the air smells like sage. The view is ridge after ridge of San Gabriel Wilderness.

At 5,300 feet, across from Charlton Flat, I find what I’m looking for: a faded stop sign, a faded five mph sign, then a crisp yellow square: STREET LEGAL ONLY. The pavement ends. Mount Mooney Road winds up between clusters of pine. The road forks. One direction is closed. I take the other and push on farther than I planned to go.

These bikes were made for exactly this. Heritage enduro. Scrambler. Adventure motorcycle. Different names for the same idea: classic looks, genuine capability, and the promise that the ride doesn’t have to end where the pavement does.

RELATED: I Thought Motorcycles Didn’t Belong in the Wilderness. I Was Wrong.

In 1980, BMW built the R 80 G/S—the first production enduro with more than one cylinder, equally at home on pavement and off it. It won the Dakar Rally four times and created a category that every brand here has since made its own. The 2026 R 12 G/S is BMW circling back to where it all started, but the segment is bigger than one bike now—and there’s an entry point for everyone.

Sources indicate that the details on these machines are more deliberate than the nostalgia suggests. Even the R 12’s round analog gauge is a choice, says Shawn McLean, product and accessories manager at BMW Motorrad USA—it puts a rider in a certain adventure mindset. “So much of motorcycling is aspirational,” he says. “It’s about the dream. What do I dream I could be? And this is a piece of how that happens.”.

Industry observers note that here are four machines to help you dream a little bigger and head somewhere you’ve never been on a Sunday afternoon. The fork I took on Mount Mooney Road was filled with pines that kept opening onto upcoming ridgelines, and somewhere past the last switchback the road turned into a dotted line on the map. I turned around in the late light, 25 miles from Los Angeles. It still felt like a thousand.

Industry observers note that if you were the kind of kid who dreamed of exploring the world on a motorcycle, you already know this bike. Spoked rims, a steel tank, and an updated 1170cc boxer engine out front where you can see it.

According to recent reports, look closer and it tells you what it wants to do, with a fully adjustable suspension, serrated foot pegs, and wheel sizes set up for adventure. The R 12 G/S shares its platform with BMW’s new roadster and cruiser—but this is the one built for dirt. BMW runs it in the GS Trophy stock, no modifications.

It has been revealed that start it and the whole bike shakes. Get moving and it finds its balance, raucous but composed. It feels like it would run forever. Like it has been running forever and has no plans to stop.

Sources indicate that this bike wants to take you somewhere that ends at a campfire with a Mezcal Negroni, wondering how you got so lucky. The V85 TT is squat, beefy, muscular in a way that’s hard to place—like it’s from a sci-fi spaghetti Western that never happened. Two round headlights, an 853cc engine that juts sideways from the frame and just thumps. Shaft drive means no chain to care for—one less thing between you and wherever you’re going.

In a recent development, the clutch has its own personality at low speeds—it wants you to learn its dance. Get that right and this thing will be your best friend. Moto Guzzis are still built in one small factory in Mandello del Lario, and it shows.

Some bikes look like they mean business. This one actually does. Those raised pipes aren’t decoration. Neither is the Ohlins rear suspension—the same brand that highlights up on MotoGP race bikes. Nothing on the Scrambler 1200 XE is there for show. The bright screen and friendly controls don’t fight the classic looks.

In a recent development, if the most iconic British off-road vehicle were a motorcycle, it would feel exactly like this. Tall and commanding. The 1200cc engine is quieter and smoother than the silhouette suggests. Matte Khaki Green is the color. Whoever buys this one says they’re taking a solo trip this weekend, and actually goes.

The Bear is compact, heavy, and metal—and more substantial than its size suggests. That weight sits low and tight, which is why it inspires confidence the moment you’re moving. The badge on the tank—a crown in yellow and silver—is applied like indices on a fine watch face.

Recent findings suggest that the 648cc parallel twin wakes up between 3,000 and 4,000 RPM and doesn’t hesitate. Showa upside-down forks up front. The clutch is smooth, the controls intuitive.

Industry observers note that the Bear invites you to point it down a dirt road with a duffel strapped to the back. It’s like that little dog that thinks it’s a big dog. All it wants to do is go anywhere you wanna go.

Sources indicate that the best roads for these bikes don’t have names, they have numbers: forest service designations, BLM routes, and fire roads that go somewhere the pavement doesn’t. California alone has over 1.1 million acres of designated off-highway riding and more than 43,000 miles of trails. Most of it sits on federal land. And California is just one state. Here’s how to find yours.

Purpose-built off-highway vehicle (OHV) parks with managed trail systems, camping, and designated routes for every skill level. California’s nine SVRAs alone cover 145,000 acres. Most states have equivalents. Your state’s parks and recreation department is the best place to start.

The U.S. Forest Service manages more than 265,000 miles of roads and trails, and 65,000 of those are dedicated to OHV use. You don’t need a dirt bike, either: street-legal motorcycles are welcome on those designated routes. Grab your maps from the Forest Service website before heading out.

Recent findings suggest that bureau of Land Management land is where the real scale lives. Millions of acres across the American West are open to designated trail or open-riding use.

Recent findings suggest that someone already mapped the best long-distance off-road riding in America. Nonprofit BDR’s network covers nearly every western state, plus many more across the country, with routes designed specifically for adventure motorcycles.

Industry observers note that to find all of it, download the Gaia GPS app. Overlay the Motor Vehicle Use Maps (MVUM Roads & Trails) and start looking for the dotted lines.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Snow on the mountains above Rollins Pass, Colorado. (Photo: SWKrullImaging via Getty).

A late fall hike turned into an overnight rescue on the Colorado section of the Continental Divide Trail on November 14 when a trio of hikers called for a rescue after encountering severe weather and wintry conditions at 11,600 feet.

It has been revealed that located about an hour and a half drive away from Denver, the High Lonesome Trail runs concurrent with part of the CDT, reaching a high point of 12,111 feet. When hiked in its entirety, it also involves 3,742 feet of elevation gain over the course of 18 miles. Recent day-time temperature highs in the area have hovered between 26 and 37 degrees, while lows were recorded at 5 and 9 degrees with wind gusts as high as 50 mph.

Grand County Search and Rescue (GCSAR), which responded, mentioned that the hikers called for help after encountering dangerous trail conditions, significant snow, and navigational struggles. The team dispatched a group of rescuers who rode ATVs up the Rollins Pass Road before dismounting and hiking the remaining distance there. When rescuers made it to the trio, they found the hikers were wet, cold, and tired.

Industry observers note that “The subjects had set up camp but lacked appropriate gear, including fire making supplies, to spend the night in the deteriorating weather,” rescue officials wrote. A second rescue team joined the party later in the evening before accompanying the hikers back to the staged ATVs and from there to the trailhead.

It has been revealed that although most of Grand County has yet to see significant snow, November can be a deceptive time of the year to hike in Colorado’s high country. Trails may appear accessible, but factors like extreme temperatures, inclement weather and reduced daylight hours can make hiking and camping more treacherous than usual.

It has been revealed that the Continental Divide Trail is the highest-elevation long trail in the United States, with its high point at the summit of 14,278-foot Grays Peak. Colorado’s section is the highest on the trail; the USFS estimates that the CDT’s average elevation across the state is 10,000 feet.

The Psychological Toll of Changing Winters on Everyday Skiers

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Outsideonline

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that last winter, Taos Ski Valley got just 76 inches of snow.
  • It has been revealed that skiing has always been an organizing principle in my life.
  • Recent findings suggest that skiing is about pleasure, and perhaps about taking a break from bills and taxes, work and chores.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last winter, Taos Ski Valley got just 76 inches of snow. It’s the leanest winter on record for the northern Newly introduced Mexico ski resort, which saw 91 inches the previous season. Both numbers are far from the annual average of about 170 inches. Whole swaths of the mountain (my home hill) remained closed until late in the season, and the resort shut down early when a warm spring made quick work of what thin snowpack remained. For the first time in my life, I rode my mountain bike in February. I admit, I’ve been a little blue.

It has been revealed that skiing has always been an organizing principle in my life. As a kid, my parents dutifully hauled four children and an impossible amount of patience into the Cascades every winter weekend. During stints in the Midwest and on the East Coast, I skied on landfills and ice sheets. I decided I could stay in Fresh Mexico forever after one good season at Taos, where winter transforms a series of steep, high-altitude ridges into endlessly compelling skiable terrain.

Recent findings suggest that skiing is about pleasure, and perhaps about taking a break from bills and taxes, work and chores. Done well, the sport can also invite deeper connection with the natural world and the seasonal cycle. Which means it has the paradoxical effect of being both a source of escapist joy and a front-row seat to a rapidly changing climate. Increasingly, a skier’s pleasure brings them closer to their pain.

In a recent development, as winters grow more unpredictable, individuals and the industry have to grow more adaptable. The wise among us are inviting in a deeper and more complex relationship with winter, one that welcomes fear, loss, and grief—casting the beauty and the joy in even sharper relief.

In a recent development, when I got on the phone with Ewan Mackie, the mountain manager at Treble Cone, the popular Upcoming Zealand ski area had just shut down for several days after a heavy snowfall followed by rain. He doesn’t hesitate to acknowledge that climate change threatens the industry.

Recent findings suggest that “You’d be bonkers to not state that as a fact, with the evidence that’s being played out,” he notes. “But I don’t believe that we are going to shut up shop in ten years. There’s a future. It’s definitely not easy. But you just have to change the way you do things.”.

He points to the increasing adoption of snowmaking technologies that allow resorts to make snow at warmer temperatures. The SnowFactory, from Italian company AlpinTech, can create snow in temperatures up to 86 degrees Fahrenheit, and man-made snow forms a denser, more durable snowpack than natural snowfall. Snowcats equipped with new technology allow operators to assess snow depth and repair shallow areas. At Treble Cone, earthworked trails protect the snow from the harshest angles of sunlight.

In a recent development, the bad weather days have offered Janina Kuzma a welcome chance to train and prepare for her final guide exams. At 40, she’s reinvented her career several times, first finding success as a competitive substantial-mountain athlete, then as a halfpipe skier. She qualified for the Olympics in 2014 and 2018, and when an injury sidelined her before her second Games, she pivoted again, beginning a years-long journey to become a fully certified backcountry ski guide.

In a recent development, kuzma’s versatility and resilience offer a framework through which anyone can shape their relationship to the sport. When the snow is lackluster, she’ll spend the day in the terrain park, on man-made snow and features. It’s better to ski a beautiful groomer than nothing at all.

“You have to make the most of every winter, whatever the conditions,” she says.

According to recent reports, ski guide Christine Feleki, who works for Bella Coola Heli Sports in British Columbia, reframes her clients’ expectations—and her own—to focus on simply having a mountain experience. In the Coast Mountains, climate change is painfully apparent: monster wildfires, glacial retreat, an increasingly difficult-to-manage snowpack. It’s also wildly stunning, and that’s enough for Feleki.

“I can have fun skiing crappy, hard boilerplate in a beautiful place,” she states.

In a recent development, we can vote and protest; we can change our habits; we can educate ourselves and others. But if you feel profoundly overwhelmed or powerless about a changing climate, that makes sense too. This is a global cataclysm. The scale is beyond what a single human mind can really comprehend. This is why bearing witness is imperative: to go and be present with the Earth as she’s changing, to try and understand.

Sources indicate that but then, of course, you will probably get a little sad. And what do you do with that?

It has been revealed that “Grief is a measure of our love, and there’s a lot that we can learn from it,” states Britt Wray, a Canadian writer and researcher focused on climate change and mental health. “It is an opening for relearning the world and our place within it as we move forward, after having recognized the difficult realities that we’re in.” Anxiety and sadness are valid, reasonable responses to what is being lost.

In a recent development, “Positive psychology that tells us certain feelings are good to have and feel, like hope, optimism, pride, love, and happiness, and that others are bad to feel, like shame, guilt, depression, grief, and anxiety,” she states. “[But] emotions are neutral and they carry information.” She encourages becoming curious about and learning to sit with difficult feelings.

It’s a tough assignment, sitting with grief on the chairlift. But mountain athletes have never been far from uncertainty and loss. Skiing is inherently ephemeral, played out on a landscape formed by a fickle and ever-changing substance. People die every year in the mountains, and plenty more return home with injuries or psychological trauma. As a community, we’re already well-equipped to bring significant-hearted depth to our relationship with the mountains. And as dutiful witnesses to ever-changing winters, we’re already practicing acceptance.

The next step is to practice something much more fun: savoring. “Studies show that taking time to savor experiences that might be going away soon can make us appreciate them more,” claims Laurie Santos, PhD, a cognitive scientist and professor of psychology at Yale, who teaches a wildly popular class on happiness. In her course, Santos talks about a process called hedonic adaptation, in which we get used to—and thus stop deriving deep pleasure from—good things. Savoring, which involves slowing down, being in the present moment, and practicing gratitude, is a powerful tool against this.

Industry observers note that “Climate change may be taking some of these activities away, and we won’t be young, fit, and able-bodied enough to enjoy them forever. I bet 90-year-old you would love skiing on powder that wasn’t perfect with the knees you have now,” she notes. “Remembering that things are finite can help us appreciate them more.”.

Sources indicate that if, on a bluebird, uncrowded powder day, you find yourself thinking This is how it should be, or I deserve this, check yourself. It’s a recipe for feeling like anything but the best is somehow wrong. The key is to reframe not just a perfect day, but the entire pursuit of skiing, as the profound privilege and gift that it is. And if the idea that someday it’s all going to end makes you nervous, just remember—that’s nothing fresh. A keen awareness of what we stand to lose makes it even sweeter.

Sources indicate that we love this project because there’s no right way to make one. Keep it simple, or get super crafty— it’s all up to your kids’ imagination. Use the guide below to get started, and decide in advance what you’ll make out of each handprint. This is much easier to do before your little helper has paint all over their hands!

Industry observers note that paint your kids’ hands with the selected colors and have them make a print on each piece of paper. Colored paper is also an option if you want to use white paint (see January and October). Depending on your design, you may need just one handprint, a fingerprint, or even a footprint. Be sure to wash and dry your hands between each month, and continue through the year, from January to December. If you think it doesn’t look like much, don’t worry! After each month has dried, and you add the details, it’ll look awesome. Insider Tip: Let your kids have some input with this project. In a recent development, now that you have all of the months ready to go (and dry!), it’s time to put your calendar together. The easiest way to go is to order a ready-made blank calendar, such as this blank wall calendar from Amazon. For under $10, you won’t have to mess with binding or stapling, or fussing with the assembly of the calendar—glue or use double-sided tape to attach your own homemade monthly pictures to the blank template and you’re good to go.

Industry observers note that print out a blank 2023 calendar from Calendar Labs. One by one, place the pages behind the handprint so that when it flips upward, you’ll have the right picture and month. For example, the calendar days for January should be glued to the February picture, the calendar days for February should be glued to March, and so on.

Insider Tip: Make sure to place the calendar month on the backside and bottom of the handprint, so as you flip each month, the painted picture is positioned the correct way.

Recent findings suggest that once you’ve glued all the calendar pages to the handprints, use the laminating sleeves to seal each one. Follow the instructions on the package, and use a ruler to eliminate any air pockets or creases.

Using a hole punch, make three holes at the top of each page (the calendar month should have the holes at the top) and one hole at the bottom (this is where the calendar will hang on the wall).

In a recent development, then, using string or thin twine, run a length through each of the three holes and tie it up like you would a book (it should open from the right side). That’s it! You’ll have a fun keepsake that will hang around for an entire year.

Sleep-Unders Are Honestly a Win for Everyone

📅 08 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (302 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins.
  • According to recent reports, the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part.
  • All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds.

Recent findings suggest that as soon as kids hit school age, the pressure of the sleepover begins. Whether your little one wants to host a crew of first graders in your living room (hard pass) or is being asked to sleep over at someone else’s house, there are a lot of questions that come with the milestone. Will my kid have fun? Will they sleep at all? Will they be overwhelmed? Add to that concerns surrounding safety, and it’s a tough position for parents to be in. The solution: the “sleep-under.”.

According to recent reports, the sleep-under brings the best elements of the sleepover and avoids the actual sleeping-over part. It’s become a trendy birthday party theme because it puts less pressure on kids and the parents hosting. How it works is that kids show up to the host house all ready for a sleepover, usually around dinner time. Guests might even arrive decked out in their coziest PJs to add to the whole sleepover vibe. The group enjoys pizza, watches a movie, plays some games, and does an activity like decorating cupcakes.

All the festivities are concluded just before bedtime, when parents return to swoop up their little ones and everyone heads back home to sleep in their own beds. Nobody is over-tired the next day. Nobody needs to call home for a late-night pickup when they have a nightmare. No parent has to stress over whether it’s a good idea to leave their kid overnight with someone they only know from the pick-up line. No kid has to feel ashamed if they aren’t yet ready to sleep away from their parents for the night. The sleep-under side-steps all those potential issues.

Honestly, it’s pretty genius. We just wish it were a thing when we were kids!

#147723. 21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1638 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tinybeans ↗ Open Full Page

21 Easy Play Ideas for Kids (Whether You Have 5, 15, or 30 Minutes)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1638 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement.
  • It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being.
  • The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that between daily parenting duties, work, and navigating the current world in general, saying your days are full is probably an understatement. And while your kid’s day may be full of exploration and creativity, they can also experience a lot of anxiety, stress, and pressure. That makes it even more crucial to have some positive, uninterrupted time to reconnect.

It has been revealed that even five minutes can make a difference in a child’s emotional well-being. But as Randy McCoy, VP of Product & Curriculum for The Little Gym, reminds us, how long you play is less important than how often. “It’s not necessarily the ‘duration of play’ but the ‘frequency of play’ that matters most,” Mccoy states. “If a parent can give their child their undivided attention and play with them just five minutes a day, every day, they’re on the right track.”.

The good news is, there are lots of ways to play that take next-to-no prep. Read on for 21 easy ideas to play with your kids, whether you have five minutes, 15, or more.

When you have a few minutes, whether it’s before school or after dinner, bust out these little-to-no-prep basics you can use just about anywhere.

1. Try out “Would You Rather?” kid edition. Spend a fun five minutes taking turns asking questions like, “Would you rather never eat ice cream again or get a trampoline?” or “Ride a dinosaur for 20 miles or an elephant for an hour?” The sillier the better. This also makes a great road trip game.

Recent findings suggest that 2. Make a dictionary dash. Grab a dictionary and choose a word at random. Read it out loud and have the kids guess what it means. If they can read, they can take turns finding words and trying to stump you.

Recent findings suggest that 3. Tickle your sidekick’s funny bone. Whip out brain busters or riddles that will make them laugh. Luckily, you don’t need Comedy Central writers for this one. We think your goofballs will get a kick out of our ultimate list of jokes for kids.

Recent findings suggest that 4. A few rounds of “We’re going on a picnic” alphabet-style will entertain the tot lot. The first player up states, “I’m going on a picnic,” then adds a tasty packable to the phrase, like an apple, apricot, or avocado. Stick with ABC order or focus on just one letter for each round.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Play 20 questions. Have your kids guess what you’re thinking of, and keep it simple, like something you can see from where you’re standing.

6. Play a classic game of Rock, Paper, Scissors—Japanese style. It’s called Janken. Start by saying “saisho wa guu.” Then “janken pon” as you pump, before throwing on “pon.” The winning combos are still the same in this timeless, quick game you can play at home or on the go.

According to recent reports, 7. Turn yourself into a living “spot the difference” puzzle. Start with a slow model turn, then disappear and make a quick change out of sight. When you come back, your cutie’s got to spot what’s different. Did you take off a cap? Put on a scarf? Untie a shoe? Keep it easy for the tots, and kick it up a notch for older kiddos (only one earring!). Then let them have a turn trying to stump you.

Sources indicate that 8. Try out a sequencing game when the wanderlust takes hold. Name a person, place, and object, all starting with the same letter of the alphabet, then string them together like kids lining up for the school bus. “Alice from Australia loves alligators!” See how far you can get in a short amount of time.

For parents, playing with our kids allows us to step out of all those daily parental duties and, as McCoy explains, build friendship between parent and child. “It provides an opportunity for you to interact with them on a different level,” he indicates. “For a special moment, you step out of the ‘parent’ role and step into a playmate role.”  Take a break from your to-do list and try one of these 15-minute ideas that will thrill the kids and relax you, too.

9. Post-It style. A stack of Post-It notes and a pen are all it takes to play this short-and-sweet variation of the classic guessing game for parties. Choose someone to be “it.” Write on the Post-It note the name of a character from a book, movie, or show that your kid will recognize—it can be a famous person, someone they know, or a fictional character. Stick the note to their forehead, without letting them see what you wrote. Now take turns going around the room giving “it” clues to help them guess who is on their head.

Sources indicate that 10. Curl up with a good book. Putting out a basket of books in a central location motivates the kids to take a look through the pages when they’ve got time to spare. Add in a sweet bookmark that keeps track of time to make it count.

11. Give them their daily feels. Keep your favorite sensory bin fillers on hand (like cotton balls and dry beans), along with trinkets to bury and cups for spilling and filling. When you’ve got a short window, pull out the bin, fill ‘er up, and watch your kids dig and drizzle until it’s time to go.

12. Set up a quick cotton ball and straw race. Perfect for the kitchen table before lunch is served. Have siblings challenge each other for the pole position on a straightaway down the center of the table, or set up a simple obstacle course using cups that the kiddos have to work around. Ready, set, go!

According to recent reports, 13. Give a penny for their thoughts when they write in a journal. Setting aside a short amount of time to write (each day!) is a great way to encourage your amateur author’s creativity. Use silly or thought-provoking prompts to get them thinking, like, “The first time I tried …” or “When I get to be principal, I’ll …” or even “The craziest thing that happened today…” Write on, brother!

Sources indicate that 14. Give up the charade. Have your little monkey stay in character when you play a quick game of animal charades. No prep is necessary for this easy guessing game. Just pick your favorite animal and go for it! With each successful guess, trade places and start again. Ee-i-ee-i-o!

Whether your aim is active playtime or quiet(er) crafting time, filling a cool 30 minutes with your kids is easier than you think. It may take a bit of planning, but once the prep is done, it’s a sit-back-and-relax situation that’s well worth the time upfront.

15. All things LEGO. If LEGO was the first thing that popped into your head, then we’re right there with you. They’re the forever fallback for a reason, but to hit that half-hour sweet spot, try throwing a LEGO challenge into the mix: building a car that can also work underwater, or constructing a tower that’s at least 24 inches tall. Then let your master-builder go to work.

According to recent reports, 16. Spin them right round. Ana at Babble Dabble Do has a latest way to play with Perler beads. She puts them to work teaching science and playing tricks when these melted beauties become spinning tops. It’s just the right amount of make-and-play to fill a brief window in your busy day.

17. One for the movers and shakers. Print out (and laminate if you’re feeling bold) The Alerting Activity Game, designed by Training Happy Hearts. Keep the deck on hand to stack the odds in your favor when the kids need something to do. With simple activities like “jump up and down ten times” or “pretend to be a volcano,” it’s packed with energy-burning activities that kids can run through on their own or with you!

Recent findings suggest that 18. Bring the outside in and paint it. If snow isn’t covering your yard, go for a hunt for leaves, evergreen boughs, and sticks. Then take your findings to the craft table to fancy them up with paint. Acrylics work great for this project.

For activities that span the hour, the two-step Make & Play approach works well. You may want to do a little prep the day before to make it easier, like putting crafting necessities into one small bin that you can pull out to surprise the kids.

19. Wage war. Ah, the classic card game that is so simple to learn and so hard to win. It is possible that a game of war can take longer than one hour, but it rarely takes less. You do two card battles with the highest card the winner until one person has all the cards. Get the complete rules here.

In a recent development, 20. Create a mini catapult. Little Bins for Little Hands has an awesome tutorial, using craft sticks and other office supplies you’re sure to have around the house. Once it’s built, set up target practice plates before letting the marshmallows fly.

21. Put on a show. Puppets never get old; they’re easy to make with an old sock, brown paper lunch bag, or even familiar characters glued to craft sticks. Whatever method you choose, spend time creating and playing with puppets when you’ve got an hour or more to spare. Be sure to stock the craft bin with all kinds of googly eyes, buttons, yarn, and doo-dads to help bring your buddies to life. Then find an old sheet or use a baby’s blanket draped over the table to create a stage. Bravo!

41 Elf on the Shelf Ideas (Because You’re Gonna Need Them)

💡 Key Takeaways

  • I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves.
  • If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it’s that time again. Yup, your Elf on the Shelf is about to parachute in to make your life (slightly) more challenging for the next few weeks. Get ahead of the game and prep your bag of tricks with these brilliant ideas. From Elf on the Shelf clothes to last-minute Elf on the Shelf ideas that’ll make the whole family giggle, we’ve got enough easy Elf ideas to last you the entire holiday season.

I remember when my kids were little, and they got their first elves. Not going to lie, remembering to move the thing every night was a struggle. But when I made the effort and managed to pull off even the easiest of Elf ideas, the look in their eyes was priceless.

1. Elf held captive. If you have two Scout elves, this easy Elf idea is a lot of fun. Pull out a toy train and a string, and decide which elf is going to be extra naughty by tying up the other one.

Sources indicate that 2. Initiative a hot cocoa party. This is fun on the first night or maybe on a weekend day. Get mugs, instant cocoa, and marshmallows set up in advance and settle the elves against the mugs. Snag printables for the party here.

3. Spell it out. Do you have Scrabble tiles or Bananagrams? Then it’s a cinch to let your elf leave a sweet message for your littles to discover the next day.

According to recent reports, 4. Caught in the act. With this easy elf idea, you’ll use a bag of M&Ms, chocolate chips, or even a box of sugar cereal, and position your elf with its backside out of the bag.

Sources indicate that 5. Exhausted elf. All those trips up to the North Pole make for one tired elf. Let your little one in red take a day off. Make them a little bed with a doll blanket and a cotton ball for a pillow.

6. Deeds worth doing. Since reporting good deeds to Santa is your elf’s duty, it’s the perfect opportunity to remind kids about the spirit of Christmas. We dig the free downloadable from Over the Big Moon.

7. Elf spaghetti. Whip up Buddy the Elf’s favorite dish for your little helper. Hint: this is a great idea for the night you make pasta. You’ll also need syrup (of course), marshmallows, candy, and chocolate syrup. Find out how to make a batch over at Instructables.

Industry observers note that 8. Riding the banister. Those naughty elves are always looking for an adrenaline rush! Use a Frisbee and sticky tape to get your little buddy set up at the top and ready to ride.

9. Sitting pretty. Have your elf take a seat inside your wreath or on the holiday table for a picture-perfect spot.

According to recent reports, 10. Play games. Set up your elf mid-move with this adorable mini-Twister printable.

11. Window view. If you’ve got a window and a curtain rod, you’ve got a sweet spot to hang your elf. Easy-peasy.

Recent findings suggest that 12. Rock climbing wall. All you need is several pre-made bows to make a route for your elf.

13. Coloring elf. Take 30 seconds to scribble in a coloring book or on a printable, scatter crayons, and set up your elf. Giggles are guaranteed!

In a recent development, 15. Zipline. This Elf on the Shelf idea is popular, but it does take a little time to set up. All you need is string or yarn, a candy cane, and a way to secure your elf to the candy cane!

16. LEGO throne. Whether you use DUPLO or LEGO, making a seat for Santa’s little helper can be done in less than five minutes.

Recent findings suggest that 17. Elf in the kitchen. Got a play kitchen? Then let your elf whip up something yummy.

18. On the road. With a toy car, your elf can go just about anywhere they want to go. Headed to buy a Christmas tree? Done. Want to take Wonder Woman out on a date? Totally!

19. Play Picasso. A dry-erase marker, a family photo, and a sense of humor are all you need. Give your kids beards and cat ears: See how much they laugh!

According to recent reports, 20. Put the elf in the freezer. Your elf sure does miss the North Pole! Give him a little time to chill.

Recent findings suggest that 21. Toilet paper tricks. Add an elf to a roll of toilet paper and send them down the stairs. Don’t have a second level? Leave a trail of written messages down the hall instead.

22. Bath time. You don’t need a Barbie bath to let your Elf soak aching bones— a plastic bowl or storage container will do the trick. Add marshmallows for bubbles, and you’re set.

23. Gone fishing. Your kids will love waking up to find the elf “fishing” for goldfish crackers in the bathroom sink.

It has been revealed that 24. Story time. Position the elf with a favorite holiday book and a captivated audience.

Recent findings suggest that 25. Hanging by a limb. Any elf will feel right at home when dangling from a branch of the Christmas tree.

26. Spa day. Wrap your elf in a paper towel, give them cucumber eye patches, and just like that, it’s a spa day.

Sources indicate that 27. Puzzle play. Settling your elf in for the night with a puzzle is easy and fun.

It has been revealed that 28. Paper bag race. Take those lunch bags that have been cluttering your drawer and collect a few stuffies. Then, stage a sack race-style scene across your dining room table or kitchen island.

29. Elfie selfie. Position your elf in front of the family laptop and snap a picture. Just be forewarned, if it’s a laptop you use, you’ll need to get it set back up before the kids get home from school.

It has been revealed that 30. Sweet snow angels. It’s not quite as cold down here as it is at the North Pole. When your elf gets antsy for chilly weather, make them a personal snow angel. You can use flour (but it’s messy), sprinkles, or rice, which is my personal favorite because it’s the easiest to clean up!

Recent findings suggest that 31. All wrapped up. Give your elf the scissors, tape, and wrapping paper. Scatter shredded paper and tape around, and it’ll be like they were caught in the act of wrapping up Santa’s gifts!

32. Elf making popcorn. Someone’s ready for family movie night!

Industry observers note that 33. Don’t move the elf. Well, it looks like your kids were so well-behaved that no North Pole reporting was needed. It’s also the perfect excuse for one of those nights you forget to move them.

According to recent reports, 34. Cards, anyone? Didn’t you know elves love to play games? They do, and they love to be caught mid-game.

35. A Stuck Elf. This is a super-easy elf idea, and you don’t even need the message board to pull it off. Just grab a mason jar or an empty water bottle and a prominent place to display your elf’s tight situation.

Industry observers note that 36. S’more to love. Some toothpicks, roasted marshmallows, chocolate squares, graham crackers, and tea lights are all you need to set up this cozy and easy elf idea.

In a recent development, 37. Read all about it. Prop them up on a favorite Christmas story or beloved book.

According to recent reports, 38. Caught red-handed. Have your elf stage a scene of questionable actions and tape up the area with crepe paper.

According to recent reports, 39. Photo editor. They can’t help but make mischief, and marking up a festive photo is a silly way to say, “Elf wuz here.”.

It has been revealed that 40. Riding dinos. If you’ve got a plastic dinosaur (T. rex preferred), then you’ve got what you need to give your elf a prehistoric ride.

41. Send the Elf back to the North Pole. Possibly one of our favorite easy elf ideas: on Christmas Morning, make sure they’re out of sight, and of course, leave a note.

The Best Way to Avoid a Meltdown When iPad Time Is Over

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (272 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, we can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them.
  • Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.
  • A few things to note about this method.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we can already feel the tension spreading through our bodies: It’s time to put away the iPad, but there is a small person who is almost certainly going to lose their mind when you tell them. Whether you resort to a countdown timer or go the “this is your last show” route, it’s pretty much always a struggle.

Perhaps you need a fresh strategy. Parenting coach Dr. Chelsey Hauge-Zavaleta recently shared her method for successfully ending iPad time, and it combines a little bit of the two approaches above with some voice modulation and sensory input.

A few things to note about this method. Using language like “We have one more song” instead of “This is our last song before we leave for school” focuses on what the child is doing now versus what you are doing in the future. It’s easier for kids to accept the transition this way.

“Melodic intonation” is when you use a sing-songy voice to make a statement. It helps kids notice what you are saying and acknowledge it. Take a look at Miss Rachel and a lot of the other preschool-focused programming, and you’ll see it employed often. Using melodic intonation for the phrase “iPad is all done” helps to signal the transition for the child.

Industry observers note that it’s vital to remember that even when using a technique like this, it will take you doing it the same way over and over several times before your child catches on and gets with the program. If they have a meltdown, don’t engage; stay calm; and move on.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If you don’t give a toddler something to do, they’ll find their own source of entertainment—and that can be a terrifying prospect (you know the feeling if you’ve suddenly noticed the house is too quiet only to find that they’ve somehow given themselves bangs). To keep them out of trouble and thoroughly entertained, we’ve rounded up some awesome games for toddlers that are sure to be a hit, whether you’re indoors or outdoors. The best part? Your kiddo won’t know it, but they offer ample opportunities for hands-on learning. Ready for endless fun? On your mark. Get set. Go find your tot’s new fave!

Toddlers are bundles of energy: always on the move, always growing, always learning. Learning with play is essential for their development because it improves small and large motor skills, muscle strength, emotional intelligence, language development, spatial awareness, and more. According to an article by Michael Yogman, MD, FAAP, on Healthychildren.org, “research shows play can improve children’s abilities to blueprint, organize, get along with others, and regulate emotions. In addition, play helps with language, math, and social skills, and even helps children cope with stress.”.

In a recent development, figuring out how to keep toddlers engaged is no easy feat. There are outdoor games, indoor games, toys, beginner board games… You get the idea. The key is to decide which activity is right for your kiddo, and that depends on factors like their age, energy level, developmental stage, and other milestones.

One of the most key things to consider is what interests your toddler. Do they love Ms. Rachel? Are they obsessed with a sport? Do they love baby dolls or animals? Once you figure out what will keep them interested, you can go from there.

Another factor is something called Play Schemas, a concept first used by Swiss psychologist Jean Piaget. As stated in My Play Cupboard, Play Schemas are repeated patterns of behaviour you notice children engaging in when they play. Nine schemas can be commonly observed in young children, including connection, transforming, enveloping, enclosing, and positioning.

Once you figure out which Play Schema your toddler is drawn to, that will help you decide what type of games they’ll enjoy the most.

In a recent development, give your jumping bean something to jump about—letters! We love that this outdoor game from The Imagination Tree combines alphabet awareness with the chance to get those wiggles out. Simply write letters in sidewalk chalk and have your little one hop from one to another as you call them out. And all you need to get started is a set of sidewalk chalk. Read all about it and check out the phonics and math variations over at The Imagination Tree.

Let your toddler be your boss with a few rounds of Simon Notes. Toddlers love the chance to be in charge! Then, you can give the commands for a bit. It's silly, active, and engaging—that's why it's an early childhood classic. Plus, it gives little ones a chance to practice following instructions, taking turns, and building listening skills. Simon Says go play!

What are the benefits of toddler games?

Playing games with your toddler is not only a great opportunity to enjoy quality time with your child, but they help develop important life skills like problem solving, small and large motor skills, physical coordination, hand-eye coordination, and learning how to be social with others.

What types of games are best for toddlers?

While it depends on your child’s age, interests, and development, the best toddler games are simple and fun. Popular ideas include pretend play, memory games, music games, and basic movements, like a simplified version of Simon Notes.

How much screen time is appropriate for toddlers?

According to the American Academy of Child & Adolescent Psychiatry, toddlers should have very limited daily screen time.

There are online toddler games that are designed specifically for young children. Parents should always review the game or content before allowing their child to watch, monitor usage, and opt for an ad-free, child-friendly tablet or platform.

What are some fun indoor games for toddlers?

Toddler indoor games should be fun and easy to set up: memory, obstacle courses, block building challenges, sensory stations, and pretend play like “the floor is lava,” “vet clinic,” and “grocery store.”.

#147716. Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (821 w)

Why You Should Fight the Urge to Make a Happy Kid Happier

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tinybeans

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • We are walking between two tractors in a barn when I say something very stupid to my 22-month-old son.
  • And then I decide to say, “Do you think the cat is in here today?”.
  • Sources indicate that last time we were here in the fall, there was a big, gray cat who got just close enough so that my toddler could bend down, reach out the tips of his fingers, and briefly graze its arched back.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We are walking between two tractors in a barn when I say something very stupid to my 22-month-old son. We’ve been at this farm for about an hour, the kind of place where you can reach your fingers through the fence to pet the goats and stare into the pigpen and marvel at how much bigger pigs are than you think. It’s a mysteriously warm winter day, and my son has thrown his jacket off, his stroller discarded somewhere around the sheep pen. For the first time in months, we are feeling the sun on our faces. He’s having the time of his life. He’s already pet a one-day-old lamb and has discovered that in the barn we are currently walking through there’s not one, not two, but three tractors.

And then I decide to say, “Do you think the cat is in here today?”.

Sources indicate that last time we were here in the fall, there was a big, gray cat who got just close enough so that my toddler could bend down, reach out the tips of his fingers, and briefly graze its arched back. But that was enough. He’d brought up the cat for days, and I knew if he saw it again, he’d be so, so happy.

Industry observers note that except there was one problem. The cat wasn’t here.

Why did I have to mention the cat? It was a perfect moment; we were like an illustration from a children’s picture book. But now, there was only one thing my son wanted to do: find the cat. I’d reminded him that there was a cat. And he loves cats. Especially this cat, the famed cat that let him touch its fur for a fraction of a second. So of course, in a very cat-like fashion, the cat was nowhere to be found.

That’s when the tears began. The three tractors were no longer enough. The baby goats—garbage. The teeny tiny lambs, only minutes ago, he was thrilled to pet. Who needs them? It was only the cat now.

Sources indicate that “I don’t know,” I noted, hoping his outburst wasn’t calling too much attention to us from the less cat-obsessed farm visitors. “He’s probably sleeping somewhere.”.

“WHERE CAT,” he demanded, over and over again.

And just like that, I’d broken my own biggest rule of parenting: Never try to make a happy kid happier.

Recent findings suggest that this rule came to me via my friend Joanna, who had learned it from her parents. As soon as she told me, I knew she’d identified one of my greatest weaknesses as a parent. I always want my son to be having a good time, and there’s some part of me that worries if I’m not actively trying to make his time better, it’s not as good as it could be.

According to recent reports, as a baby, if he was enjoying gnawing on a particular teether, I’d jump in to give him another one, too. Oh, he likes the dog at this park? Let’s leave this park with one dog to find a dog park full of dogs. If he were having a perfectly nice time throwing rocks in a puddle, I’d offer to find him better rocks that would make an even bigger splash.

There’s an impulse in us as parents not just to nurture, to make sure all gaps are closed. We want to provide the complete package for our kids, to make sure all their needs are met in the best possible way. And that urge is good. It’s why we don’t abandon them in the woods when they won’t stop crying at 4 a.m. and why we keep feeding them every day even when they throw everything we offer on the floor. But it also means we can fail to notice when we aren’t needed.

What “don’t make a happy kid happier” does is remind me that sometimes, just being happy is enough. Kids live in a world of the immediate now, where whatever they are doing is often the only thing on their minds. Yes, there might be bigger, splashier rocks to throw in the puddle, but the rocks they have in their hand suit them just fine. What I think I’m doing when I do this is helping my son, but what I’m actually doing is pointing out that what he’s doing might not be good enough. Suddenly he can see that the emperor has no clothes, and it actually becomes not good enough.

We never did find the cat. But I paid the price for my misstep in toddler currency: a temper tantrum. He settled down eventually, and by the time we left the farm, he was happily kicking and chatting in his stroller. I thought about stopping for ice cream at the gift shop, but I decided against it this time. He was just fine.
